of those runs in a process where `httpapi.Server` is **never constructed**
(cmd/api skips it at `VIDRA_ROLE=worker`). A handler-level call would have
covered the creator's upload and quietly missed the repair worker, which is the
one that runs over a whole catalogue. `video.WithMediaReplacedHook` covers all
four call sites by construction and fences on public+published — the resolver's
own `Eligible` — so a private video's poster replacement still spends nothing.

**The image URL is purged, not versioned.** The brief offered the choice; the
header table from slice 1 settles it. Both assets sit at `max-age=300,
must-revalidate` on both sides of the edge, so a purge closes the whole window
and there is no year-long immutable entry to strand — unlike an HLS child,
where `?v=` is load-bearing precisely because the entry lives for a year.
Stamping a tag on `/videos/{id}/thumbnail` would also be a **contract change**
to the URL the frontend, the feeds, oEmbed, ActivityPub and every share link
already name: the untagged URL would keep being requested and would still need
purging, so the tag would buy nothing and cost compatibility. And three
families (avatar, banner, playlist cover) already invalidate a stable URL; a
fourth with a different mechanism would be two answers to one question.

**A walk is not a transaction.** When a batch of the download revocation has a
URL the edge refuses, the cursor advances anyway and the refusals are re-queued
as their own retry job. One video the edge keeps rejecting must not hold the
other thirteen thousand hostage; what the walk row keeps is `url_set_complete`,
so "the walk finished" and "the walk finished cleanly" stay different answers
(`TestWalkRejectionsBecomeTheirOwnRetryAndDoNotStallTheWalk`).

### The queue, migration 0137

Both queued families and every retry share one durable table, `cdn_purge_jobs`,
in the shape `account_exports` (0057) already uses: `pending → running → done |
failed`, `attempts`/`next_attempt_at`/`last_error`, claimed under
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. One difference from 0057, and it is the resumability:
**`next_attempt_at` IS the lease**, so the claim admits `running` as well as
`pending` and a worker killed mid-walk simply has its row picked up again when
the lease passes — no separate recovery sweep. The walk's `cursor_video_id` is
persisted per page, which is what a restart resumes from; a partially
successful URL job **rewrites** its `urls` column to only what is still
unpurged, so a retry never re-issues a call the edge already accepted and the
column doubles as the record of exactly what may still be stale.

What the table stores is this API's own **route paths**
(`/api/v1/videos/<id>/thumbnail`), never a purge endpoint and never an edge URL.
`media_purge.go` refuses to *log* a path because the operator-supplied purge
template can carry a credential in its query string; that argument does not
reach a column whose every component is already a column of this database, and
the `DELIVERY_CDN_PURGE_*` configuration never leaves `internal/cdn`.

The worker (`runCDNPurgeWorker`, 10 s ticker, one claim per tick) is **not**
leader-gated — every claim is a lease under SKIP LOCKED, and a takedown is
exactly the work that must not wait for an election — and it starts only when a
CDN is configured, so an edgeless install runs no ticker and pays nothing.

### The retry schedule, and what an operator can expect

The immediate pass counts as attempt 1. After it, `internal/retry.Backoff` with
**base 1 minute, cap 1 hour, 8 attempts** gives seven persisted retries:

| retry | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| after | 1 m | 2 m | 4 m | 8 m | 16 m | 32 m | 60 m |

That is **123 minutes** of wall clock before a job dead-letters — so the honest
sentence is: a transient edge failure self-heals within about two hours, and
anything that has not healed by then is on the dead-letter list with its URL
list intact, at which point **nothing will try again** and the edge keeps the
object until a TTL Vidra does not set. The values are the channel-sync
backoff's shape (`interval × 2^(n-1)`, capped) with a base chosen against this
failure: one minute is far longer than any transient 5xx and far shorter than a
CDN's own default TTL. A successful retry completes the job and empties its URL
list (`TestSuccessfulRetryClearsTheRecord`).

**What the operator sees**, in three places:

* `GET /api/v1/admin/system` → `cdn_purge` now carries `pending_retries`,
  `oldest_pending_seconds` and `dead_letters` beside the existing in-process
  counters. The two halves have different lifetimes and the field names say so:
  `runs`/`keys_purged`/`keys_failed`/`last_incomplete_run_at` are reset by a
  restart, the three new ones are read from the queue and are not.
* the admin jobs page → `cdn_purge_jobs` is an eighth queue in `jobstatus`,
  with depth, oldest-pending age and dead letters in the merged failures list
  (job id and a status summary only — never a URL).
* `vidra doctor` → a new **cdn purge backlog** state check: ⚠ when anything has
  dead-lettered (*"nothing will try again"*, with the manual-invalidation fix
  and a pointer at `DELIVERY_CDN_PURGE_URL`), ⚠ when the backlog is older than
  three hours (the ladder's own ceiling plus room for a long walk), ✓ otherwise.
  A database predating 0137 is a ✓, not a skip: nothing can be pending.

### The ledger, and the residual

`media_purge.go`'s **STILL UNPURGED list is empty.** The two closed entries are
kept as `(CLOSED)` notes rather than deleted, so a reader arriving from an older
revision can see where they went. `url_set_complete` (renamed from
`key_set_complete` in slice 1) now carries three causes rather than two: a
listing failure, the per-video cap, and a superseded generation still in the
store — plus, for the account family, a channel or video listing that failed
mid-snapshot, and for the walk, a batch with an unreadable row or a refused URL.

The two unrecoverable cases slice 1 recorded were re-examined and **both stay
residual**, because neither is surgical:

* **A superseded generation's `?v=` tags.** The tag is the promoted playlist's
  own `updated_at`, and nothing records it once the row moves on. Keeping it "in
  the purge snapshot at promotion time" would mean a new column written on every
  promotion and read only by a takedown — and it would still be wrong for a
  video promoted twice, because there is one previous tag and N superseded
  generations. **Operator remedy:** the URLs stop existing when media GC
  collects the generation (`MEDIA_GC_ENABLED`); until then they are reported
  through `url_set_complete=false` on any takedown of that video. Generation-
  addressed output (0136) makes this bound shrink rather than grow.
* **A channel handle rename** strands `/api/v1/channels/<old>/avatar` and
  `/banner`. Snapshotting the old handle's URLs before the rename IS surgical
  and was written up — and then not done, because it is a *different* family
  from the four this slice was scoped to and would have added a fifth purge
  trigger with its own tests. **Operator remedy**, now in `docs/operations.md`:
  invalidate those two URLs by hand at the provider after renaming a channel on
  a CDN-fronted instance. It is recorded as a bounded follow-up rather than
  claimed.

### Gates

Only vidra-core changed, plus this repo's docs and vidra-user's generated
contract. `make ci` is **green**: `fmt-check`, `vet`, `migrate-lint` (**137** up
migrations clean), `openapi-verify`, `sqlc-verify` and `test-race` all pass —
84 `ok` packages, 0 FAIL. `go vet -tags=integration ./...` is clean.

**The integration lane WAS run**, and it had to be, because three of the
queue's properties are database behaviours no fake can show and each fails only
in production: the walk's `ON CONFLICT` inference must land on 0137's partial
unique index (a mismatch is an ERROR, so an admin's second click on the
downloads toggle would be a 500 rather than a no-op), the claim must reclaim a
`running` row past its lease (the one deviation from the `account_exports`
shape, and the only thing that stops a worker dying mid-walk from stranding it
forever), and `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` must give two concurrent claimers
disjoint rows. Six new tests in `internal/store/cdn_purge_jobs_integration_test.go`
cover those plus the two catalogue reads the walk derives its work from, which
have no fake anywhere and would otherwise never be parsed by a real planner.
Run against a **throwaway native PostgreSQL 16.15** (no container runtime — the
lab and Docker are another executor's this session), migrated to **schema 137**:
all six pass, `go test -tags=integration -race ./internal/store/` is green
whole, and 0137's `down.sql` drops the table and its three indexes cleanly and
the `up` re-applies. The cluster was torn down afterwards. The OpenAPI
contract DID change (the `cdn_purge` block), so vidra-user #197 carries the
regeneration and must merge **after** core #202; `npx tsc --noEmit` passes on it
and no component changed. In this repo `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p
'*_test.py'` is **42 tests OK, zero skips**; no compose or env file was touched,
so the prod render is unchanged from the section above.

### Unverified, and named rather than skipped

**Edge simulator re-run pending (slice 3).** Every claim above is a unit or
integration assertion. The database half was measured — see the gates — but
**nothing here was measured against a caching edge or a browser**, and in
particular: that a poster replacement makes the edge return the new bytes, that
an account deletion empties the edge, that the revocation walk covers a real
catalogue, and that a rejected purge is accepted on a later attempt are all
**argued from the code and its tests**, not observed. The selected edge and the
selected bucket stay deferred. Slice 3 must re-run the A32/A33 lab against this
branch and re-measure the per-family purge counts, the failed-purge retry, and
the stale-segment clause.

### Findings

1. **Clause (4) of INT-10 is untouched by this slice and stays open.** A 307 to
   an edge that then 5xxs has no fallback to the api proxy: the resolver's
   fail-open discipline covers *building* a source, not a viewer's fetch failing
   afterwards, and the api cannot learn about the latter. The only remedy
   remains the `delivery_cdn_enabled` kill switch. It was not in this slice's
   scope and is not fixed.
2. **The new `cdn_purge` fields are not rendered anywhere.** vidra-user's
   `AdminSystemStatusView` shows the three in-process counters and ignores
   `pending_retries`, `oldest_pending_seconds` and `dead_letters` — so today a
   dead letter is visible only in the JSON, on the jobs page's depth gauge, or
   through `vidra doctor`. Bounded follow-up for vidra-user.
3. **`docs/operations.md`'s cache-header paragraph was stale from slice 1** and
   is corrected here: it still said every media response is `private` and that
   "nothing calls Purge automatically yet", both of which stopped being true
   when #199 promoted the edge's own origin fetch to `public`. Noticed only
   because this slice had to rewrite the paragraph below it.
4. **`internal/mediaroute` is new**, and it is a move rather than an addition:
   the pure media-route path builders left `internal/httpapi` unchanged so the
   purge worker can build the same URLs in a process where no HTTP server
   exists. `httpapi` keeps one-line aliases, so no call site moved, and
   `TestMediaPathsMatchTheirRoutes` still asserts every builder against its
   route registration from inside the package that owns the router.

## A26 live RTMP — ingest, watch, moderation, replay — 2026-09-08

**INT-01 moves from BLOCKED to FAIL.** The ingest-plane selection the row was
blocked on is ruled — the owner ruled on 2026-09-08 that live RTMP is
launch-required and that the plane is the **bundled** `media`-profile service —
so the lab has run, and one clause of this row's own procedure is now measured
as unmet while the plane itself needed five defects fixed before any of the rest
could be measured at all. One PR:
[core #205](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/205). **No migration**
(core stays at schema 136) and `api/openapi.yaml` is unchanged, so there is no
`contract-ci` ordering with vidra-user. SCP-05 (full chat, slow mode, tips, DVR)
stays deferred. [Sanitized evidence](evidence/a26-live.json).

Measured on a one-origin lab — a pipe-only proxy on `127.0.0.1:8099` in front of
a production Next standalone server and a two-process vidra-core (`VIDRA_ROLE=api`
on `:8088` and a separate `VIDRA_ROLE=worker`) over native postgres 16 at schema
136 and native redis — with the bundled ingest actually running: `alfg/nginx-rtmp`
(nginx 1.23.1 + Arut's nginx-rtmp-module, linux/amd64 under emulation) in Docker,
serving the **shipped** `deploy/media/nginx.conf.template` with exactly two lines
changed, both the shim's api upstream, pointed at a transparent logging proxy so
the hook contract could be read verbatim. The publisher is `ffmpeg` 8.1 with
audio — `-re -f lavfi -i testsrc2 -f lavfi -i sine … -c:v libx264 -c:a aac -f flv
rtmp://…/<key>` — and the viewer is real Chromium. Rate limiting was **off**, so
the zero 429s is not a limits observation.

**What the shipped plane did before anything was changed: nothing worked.** The
first real publish flipped the stream `live`, the api advertised an `hls_url`,
the stream appeared on the public "Live now" rail — and the watch page rendered
no `<video>` at all, only *"Can't play this live stream / Your browser could not
play the live video feed."* beside a LIVE badge, because
`GET /live/{id}/hls/master.m3u8` answered **404** for the entire broadcast. Every
segment and playlist on disk was named `nyLJxYZ…-0.ts` — the **raw stream key**,
the credential the design says never touches the volume. And when the publisher
disconnected, the api logged *"live replay: no recording for finished session"*:
`<LIVE_HLS_ROOT>/rec` did not exist and never had.

**The hook contract, read off the wire.** nginx-rtmp callbacks cannot set
headers, so both hooks go to a shim inside the ingest container that injects
`X-Ingest-Secret` and proxies to the api. Both are
`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POSTs carrying
`app, flashver, swfurl, tcurl, pageurl, addr, clientid, call, name, type`.

| hook | `call` | `name` carries | accepted | refused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /live/ingest/start` | `publish` | the **raw stream key**, always | `302` with `Location: <stream id>` | `404` unknown key, `403` policy, `401` bad secret, `404` when `LIVE_INGEST_SECRET` is unset |
| `POST /live/ingest/stop` | `publish_done` | the **pre-rename** name — the raw key on the `live` application, the **stream id** on the `hls` application | `204` | `404` unresolvable |

That single row about `name` is the whole story of two of the defects below.

**Defect 1 — the rename never happened, so the key went to disk and playback
404d.** The hook answered `Location: rtmp://localhost/live/<id>`, and
nginx-rtmp branches on the header value itself: a value that does **not** start
with `rtmp://` becomes the session's new name, one that **does** is a PUSH RELAY
target. The ingest log says it plainly — `notify: push '<key>' to
'rtmp://localhost/live/<id>'` then `relay: no address`. Nothing was renamed and
the module tried to dial itself. The Location is now the bare id, and the ingest
log reads `notify: publish redirect to '<id>'`. The unit test that should have
caught this asserted `strings.HasSuffix(loc, "/"+id)` — which the broken value
satisfies; it now asserts the bare id and that the value is not an `rtmp://` URL.

**Defect 2 — the rename still could not reach HLS.** With the bare Location the
**recording** became `<id>-<unixtime>.flv` while the HLS stayed keyed by the raw
key, because nginx-rtmp runs its publish handlers in reverse module order: the
record module is declared before the notify module and therefore runs after it,
the HLS module is declared after and therefore runs before. No Location value
can fix that. The `live` application now `push`es the already-renamed session
into a second, loopback-only `hls` application that does nothing but package, so
the HLS module sees the stream id like everything else. `hls` accepts a publish
from `127.0.0.1` and nowhere else, so a streamer cannot reach it and bypass the
auth hook. After the change the disk reads `<id>-0.ts … <id>.m3u8` and the master
playlist answers **200**.

**Defect 3 — replay had never run, and an empty directory was why.** nginx-rtmp
does not create a missing `record_path`. Creating it at container start is not
enough either: `record_path` sits inside `hls_path`, and the HLS cleanup that
reclaims stale fragments walks the tree and `rmdir()`s empty subdirectories —
measured removing a bare `rec` **12 seconds** after start, long before any
streamer could publish into it. The compose `media` command now creates the
directory *and* plants a `.keep`, and the ingest log shows the cleanup failing
against it exactly as intended: `hls: cleanup rmdir() failed on '/data/hls/rec'
(39: Directory not empty)`. `.keep` is invisible to both sides — the cleanup only
deletes `.m3u8`/`.ts`, and the api's recording store only accepts
`<stream-id>*.flv|.mp4`.

**Defect 4 — a key rotation orphaned the session.** Rotating mid-broadcast is
what the row asks to be exercised, and it is what broke the lifecycle: the stop
hook carries the **pre-rename** name, so after a rotation that key no longer
resolved, the api answered `404 no live stream for that key`, and the stream sat
`live` for **twenty minutes** with no replay ever produced — until the duration
watchdog eventually closed it. The stop hook now lives on the `hls` application,
whose session is named by the id from the first frame; a rotation followed by a
disconnect ended the stream cleanly and published its replay. The cost is stated
in the template: the end-of-session signal now depends on the loopback push
having been established.

**Defect 5 — two ways past the stream key.** Details are deliberately thin here
and in the PR. The public stream id was accepted as a publish identity, and the
id is public — the anonymous `GET /live/{id}` and the "Live now" rail both hand
it out. And a **deactivated** owner (the A16 account block, whose token is dead
everywhere else: `GET /me` 404, login 403) kept publishing: the stream went
`live`, the playlist served **200**, and the instance listed the blocked creator
on the **public** rail. The RTMP boundary authenticates a key, not a session, so
neither could be caught by middleware. Both are refused at the publish boundary
now — the id outright unless the session is already live, the blocked owner with
a typed `403 stream owner is blocked` — and both refusals were re-run against the
real ingest: the publisher is dropped and the state stays `offline`.

**SC1, authorization and the stream key — passes.** A publish with a wrong key is
refused at the hook (`404 no live stream for that key`), nginx-rtmp drops the
connection about 100 ms after connect, ffmpeg exits 251 `Input/output error`, and
**zero bytes** reach `LIVE_HLS_ROOT`. The right key is accepted, renamed and the
row goes `live`. Rotation returns `200` with a new key and the ingest URL; the
**current publisher is allowed to finish** — it is not disconnected, segments
keep being written and the state stays `live` — while the **old key is refused on
its next publish**. The key itself is well fenced: it appears in no list body,
viewer U gets `404` on `POST /live/{id}/key` and `403` on the channel's stream
list, an **admin** also gets `404` (the routes are owner-scoped), and anonymous
gets `401`.

**SC2, the live watch — passes on playback, and answers the ladder and latency
questions with facts the row will not like.** An anonymous viewer's
`currentTime` advanced **29.0 s** across a 45.7 s window at 1280×720, with the
element unmuted at full volume, 937 frames decoded and 26 dropped, audio decoded
bytes climbing 36 305 → 510 496, and an AudioContext analyser reading a steady
RMS of **0.125** — decoded *and* non-silent, which the byte counter alone does
not prove. The playlist is a real live playlist: a moving `EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE`,
no `EXT-X-ENDLIST`, a 2 s target duration inside a 12 s window, served
`application/vnd.apple.mpegurl` and `private, max-age=0, must-revalidate`.

The **ladder is one rendition and there is no ABR**: `master.m3u8` contains
**zero** `EXT-X-STREAM-INF` lines — it *is* the media playlist — and a segment
probes as exactly what the publisher pushed (h264 Constrained Baseline 1280×720
30 fps, AAC-LC 48 kHz mono at 131 kbps). The ingest transcodes nothing, so the
"selected ladder" for live is whatever the streamer's encoder happens to emit, on
one bitrate, for every viewer. The **latency**, read from the timecode
`testsrc2` burns into the frame against the encoder's own source-time anchor, is
**9.13 s at join** — consistent with 2 s fragments and a three-fragment live
edge — and **26.36 s** forty-five seconds later, because the media clock ran at
about 0.64× while the buffer grew from 14 s to 60 s and nothing ever resynced to
the edge. The slow clock is this lab's CPU starvation (a software-rendered
headless Chromium beside an x86-emulated ingest and a native x264 encoder) and
should not be read as a product measurement; that **nothing pulls a drifted
viewer back to the live edge** is a product observation, and it is why the second
number is 17 s worse than the first.

**SC3, moderation — FAILS, and it is the clause that decides this row.** There is
**no control anywhere that terminates a live stream.** Core registers no
`/admin/live*` route; the admin's only live surface is `/admin/config/live`,
which is settings. `DELETE /live/{id}` and `PATCH /live/{id}` are owner-scoped
and answer **404** to an admin. So a moderator watching an instance-damaging
broadcast can change a global setting, delete the account, or nothing.

The one lever that does work is the global watchdog, and it was exercised for
real: `live_max_duration_secs` set to 60 (its minimum — the setting refuses
anything between 1 and 59), a publish started, and the session force-closed at
**85 s** — the limit plus up to one 30 s sweep. The state flipped to `ended`, the
playlist began answering **404** immediately, the stream dropped off every
listing, and the audit trail carries
`content.live.force_close / success / system / "stream=<id> max_duration_secs
exceeded"`. The **publisher was not disconnected**: the ingest socket lingered
and kept writing segments and its recording, exactly as `SweepOverdueLive`'s own
comment says it would, and when the publisher eventually stopped, the ordinary
stop path ran and published the replay. The blocked-creator clause **now** passes
because this slice fixed it; before the fix it failed completely.

**SC4, disconnect → replay — passes.** The mechanism is a session recording, not
promoted HLS: nginx-rtmp records to `<LIVE_HLS_ROOT>/rec/<id>-<unixtime>.flv`,
and on the stop hook the api opens the newest recording for that stream and
pushes it through the ordinary video pipeline. A publisher SIGKILLed 14 s into a
broadcast produced `ended`, a 404 on the live playlist, a recording on disk and a
replay video titled *"A26 final (replay)"* — **15 s** long, `published`, public,
on the stream's own channel — whose `job_runs` row is a `video_transcode` stamped
with both a `correlation_id` and a `request_id`. Real Chromium then played it as
an ordinary VOD: a CMAF master with **three** variants, 9 segment requests all
200, the 854×480 rendition decoding 184 frames with **0** dropped and audio
decoding alongside. There is **no grace window** — the state flips on the stop
hook — and re-publishing with the same key restarts the **same stream row** as a
**new session** with a fresh `started_at`; an `ended` one-shot stream is fully
reusable.

**SC5, hooks alone are insufficient — passes.** A hook with a wrong secret, and a
hook with no secret header at all, are both **401 `invalid ingest secret`**,
logged with a correlation id, with no state change. A hook with the *correct*
secret and a valid key but **no RTMP publish** does flip the row `live`, does
publish an `hls_url` and does put the stream on the public "Live now" rail — but
the playlist answers **404**, and the watch page renders **no `<video>` element
at all**, only the explicit *"Can't play this live stream"* state. Nothing is
faked. What the hook alone *can* do is advertise a dead stream on a public rail,
which is a finding rather than a pass/fail.

**SC6, capability truth — half passes, and the missing half is an operator
blind spot.** With the ingest configured, `/instance` reports `features.live`
**true** and create returns 201. With `LIVE_RTMP_URL` unset the derived default
takes `live_enabled` to false, `features.live` is **false**, and create is
**403 `feature_disabled`**; turning the setting explicitly on with no ingest
gives **503 `live_not_configured`** as a typed error whose sentence naming both
variables survives the 5xx scrubber. In Chromium, the Studio's Live-streams
header with live unavailable is down to just **Reload** with no create control
anywhere on the page, while the creator's existing streams stay listed and
manageable. But **`/admin/system` has no live or ingest component at all**: ten
components (`clamav`, `ffmpeg`, `mfa_kek`, `postgres`, `redis`, `s3`, `search`,
`settings_sync`, `smtp`, `storage`) and not one watches the RTMP plane, so a dead
ingest leaves the instance reading `"status":"ok"` while every publish is refused
and every viewer stares at a dead player. `/admin/infrastructure` echoes
`live.rtmp_url` and `live.hls_root` and a `configured: true` flag, but that is
config, not a probe.

**What failed first.** The very first publish, before any code was touched: the
watch page could not play a stream the API said was live, and the filename on
disk was the streamer's own secret.

**Gates.** vidra-core `make ci` — fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint, openapi-verify,
sqlc-verify, test-race — **exit 0**, 81 packages ok. vidra-user and vidra-search
were not touched, so their gates were not run and nothing here claims they were.

**Unverified.** No OBS or other real streaming client was used (ffmpeg was the
publisher). The compose `media` profile was not brought up as a profile — the
service definition was rendered and its command reproduced by hand against the
same image and the same shipped template. There was no second concurrent viewer,
and the simultaneous-live caps (`live_max_instance_lives`,
`live_max_user_lives`) were not exercised. No TLS, no real hostname, and no
ingest reachable from another machine. The replay landed on **local** storage;
S3 was not exercised.

**Findings that need a ruling rather than a patch, none blocking this verdict.**
There is **no way for a moderator to end a broadcast**, and the only lever that
exists — `live_max_duration_secs` — is global, has a 60 s floor, cuts at up to
one sweep interval late, and never disconnects the publisher, who keeps consuming
ingest bandwidth and disk. Live audit rows leave `resource_id` **empty** and put
the stream id in free-text `reason`, so the audit filter cannot target a stream.
Session recordings are **never deleted** after their replay publishes — six
`.flv` files totalling 66 MB were still on the volume when the lab ended, on a
volume the operations doc says is not backed up but says nothing about growth. A
hook-only flip puts a stream with **no bytes behind it** on the public rail.
There is no viewer count on a live stream (the card contract says so in a
comment) and no live ABR ladder, so a mobile viewer on a bad connection gets the
streamer's full bitrate or nothing. And the ingest image is pinned to
**`alfg/nginx-rtmp:latest`** — an unpinned tag whose current build is from 2022 —
for a component the owner has just made launch-required.

The lab was torn down: every process, the database cluster, the Redis server and
the ingest container were started by this session in a scratch directory; the
`live_max_duration_secs` and `live_enabled` overrides made during the lab were
reset to their defaults and the deactivated test account was reactivated.
Credentials, stream keys, the recordings and the raw logs stay outside the repo.

## A29 remediation — federated playback, dereferenceable ids, social parity — 2026-09-08

**INT-05 is NOT flipped, and this section is not the evidence that would flip
it.** Every clause of that row's verdict was measured against two live
instances, and this slice ran neither: no second instance, no caching edge, no
running Caddy, and no browser pointed at a live backend. (A real PostgreSQL
16.15 and a real Chromium DID run — the migrations were applied rather than
linted, and the mocked Playwright suite drove the frontend against route mocks;
neither is a federation lab.) What it is: the code for the three failing clauses
of that verdict, for the four findings the row recorded without letting them
decide it, and for the three the evidence file carried beyond the row — proved
by unit and integration tests. The two-instance re-run that re-measures them is
a later slice. Complete result:
[`a29-remediation.json`](evidence/a29-remediation.json). The code is
[vidra-core #203](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/203),
[vidra-user #198](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/198) and this
repo's Caddyfile change.

### The CORS ruling, which is what made a stream link emittable at all

A29's playback failure had two walls behind it and only the first was about
ActivityPub. The second was that A's media answered 200 anonymously with **no
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`**, so an HLS master fetched cross-origin by
hls.js would have been blocked even if the link had been emitted. Emitting one
without the header would have shipped a URL that cannot work.

The rule is one line, and it derives from the pair the cache policy already
uses: a media response carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` exactly when it
is **public** (the route's own eligibility assertion — the same boolean
`internal/delivery` uses to decide whether the bytes may be redirected or
shared-cached) and **non-credentialed** (no `?pt=`, no `Authorization`, no
video-read cookie in use).

| request | Cache-Control | Access-Control-Allow-Origin |
|---|---|---|
| public HLS master / variant playlist | `private, max-age=…` (unchanged) | `*` |
| public HLS segment, CMAF chunk | `private, …` (unchanged) | `*` |
| public thumbnail, storyboard.jpg/.vtt, caption | `private, max-age=300, must-revalidate` | `*` |
| public `/original`, `/webm`, `/download/*` | `private, max-age=3600, must-revalidate` | `*` |
| public live HLS (privacy `public` only) | `private, …` | `*` |
| avatar / banner / playlist cover / instance logo | `private, max-age=300, must-revalidate` | `*` |
| **private** video, any route | `private, no-store` | **none** |
| **unlisted** video, any route | `private, …` | **none** |
| **unpublished** (draft) video | `private, no-store` | **none** |
| any route with `?pt=` | `private, no-store` | **none** |
| any route with `Authorization` | `private, no-store` | **none** |
| the presigned or CDN **307 itself** | `private, max-age=300, must-revalidate` | **none** |
| the edge's own origin fetch (public object) | `public, …` (A33) | `*` |
| the edge's own origin fetch (non-public object) | `private, …` | **none** |

Three of those rows are decisions rather than consequences.

**The 307 carries nothing.** A browser re-runs the CORS check against the
redirect's TARGET, so the header that decides is the bucket's or the edge's;
putting one on the redirect would advertise an access the target may not honour.

**The edge's own fetch DOES carry it**, which is what makes a cross-origin
player work through the edge as well as against the origin: that request takes
the api-proxy path, so the wildcard is baked into the shared cache entry. It is
the same `Eligible` boolean, so a non-public object answered on the edge path
still carries neither a shared policy nor a CORS header — the marker is not a
credential and buys nothing (A33).

**Unlisted is refused**, deliberately. Unlisted media is reachable by its own
URL to a viewer who holds it and is never enumerable and never federated, so it
has no cross-origin audience to serve.

**Preflight.** hls.js fetches CMAF byte ranges with a `Range` header, which is
not a CORS-safelisted request header, so a cross-origin player preflights.
A32 measured ZERO preflights for the same-origin-then-307 case — correctly,
because a same-origin request never preflights, which is exactly why this had to
be added deliberately rather than assumed present. An OPTIONS on a media route
answers 204 with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, HEAD`,
`Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Range` and a ten-minute `Max-Age`.

The mechanism is worth stating because it is not the obvious one. Echo's CORS
middleware terminates every preflight itself, before any route handler, so a
route-level answer is unreachable. `mediaPreflight` therefore runs **before** it
and PRE-SEEDS the wildcard answer for the media routes; when the browser's
Origin is on the operator's allow-list the middleware overwrites it with the
credentialed answer (explicit origin + `Allow-Credentials`, which cookie-mode
media reads need), and when it is not, the middleware returns its 204 leaving
the wildcard in place. One middleware, both cases, and no second copy of the
allow-list matcher.

`Vary: Origin` is not added: the value is a constant, not a reflection of the
request's Origin. Echo's CORS middleware adds one of its own to every response
it sees, which is pre-existing and untouched here.

### The outbound Video, which is the whole of A29-F1

A29 found the cause on the WRITE side: `videoLinks()`, `iconURL()` and
`parseISODurationSeconds()` were all already correct, while `videoObject()`
emitted a bare-string `url`, no `icon` and no `duration` — so a vidra→vidra
federation could not populate `stream_url`, `thumbnail_key` or
`duration_seconds` no matter how good the reader was.

```json
{
  "id": "https://videos.example/videos/<uuid>",
  "type": "Video",
  "name": "…", "content": "…",
  "attributedTo": "https://videos.example/video-channels/<handle>",
  "duration": "PT367S",
  "published": "2026-08-30T08:00:00Z",
  "updated": "2026-09-02T11:30:00Z",
  "icon": { "type": "Image", "mediaType": "image/jpeg",
            "url": "https://videos.example/api/v1/videos/<uuid>/thumbnail" },
  "url": [
    { "type": "Link", "mediaType": "application/x-mpegURL",
      "href": "https://videos.example/api/v1/videos/<uuid>/hls/master.m3u8" },
    { "type": "Link", "mediaType": "text/html",
      "href": "https://videos.example/v/<short code>" }
  ],
  "to": ["https://www.w3.org/ns/activitystreams#Public"]
}
```

`id` is untouched and stays `/videos/{uuid}` forever — moving it would
re-identify every video on every peer and orphan every reply. `url` is a Link
ARRAY, PeerTube's convention and the shape vidra's own ingest already reads.
`icon` is an Image object so `mediaType` travels with the poster; width and
height are **omitted deliberately** because vidra records the VIDEO's dimensions
(`video_metadata`) and never the poster's, and inventing them would be worse
than omitting them.

**Every field is omitted when the fact behind it is absent.** No ready ladder,
no stream link; no poster, no icon; no probe, no duration. An empty `icon` or a
`PT0S` duration would be a claim the origin cannot back, and the reader would
faithfully store it. The golden fixtures now pin BOTH shapes — the finished
video and one still transcoding.

**When `Create` fires, and why an `Update` had to be added.** The publish hook
fires the `Create`, and for every video that is not `publish_after_transcode`
that is BEFORE the transcode finishes — so the `Create` necessarily carries no
stream link. Without a second activity a follower would hold a link-out-only
copy of every such video forever, which is precisely what A29 measured. The
transcode completion hook now fires `UpdateVideo`, **last** in the chain: after
`releaseHold`, because a publish-after-transcode video is not public+published
until the hold is released and `UpdateVideo` reads the video's CURRENT
privacy/state — running it first would either skip the video or actively
unfederate it. `composeTranscodeCompletion` is a pure function and a test pins
the order `[release, mirror, federate]`.

`GetVideoByID` and `ListChannelOutboxVideos` gained the three facts this needs
(duration, poster + its media type, a ready ladder) on the row the caller
already fetches; one builder renders both the delivered object and the outbox
one, and a test asserts they are byte-identical, so a peer that discovers a
video by walking the outbox and a peer that received the push cannot disagree.

The loop is closed by driving a REAL emitted activity through the REAL ingest
parsers, not through a fixture either side could drift from: `videoLinks` finds
the HLS master, `iconURL` finds the poster, `parseISODurationSeconds` reads 367.

### Dereferenceable ids, and the routing decision they needed

An ActivityPub object id is a promise: GET it with an AP `Accept` and the object
comes back. Vidra broke it for the two ids it mints most, because both live on
paths the FRONTEND owns.

| id | Accept | answer |
|---|---|---|
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `application/activity+json` | 200 AS `Video`, `ETag`, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `application/ld+json; profile="…activitystreams"` | the same (this is what Mastodon sends) |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | anything else (`text/html`, `*/*`) | **406**, as every other AP route already answers |
| `/videos/{uuid}` of a private, unlisted or unpublished video | AP | **404** — identical to a uuid that was never a video |
| `/videos/{uuid}` of a DELETED video | AP | **410 + Tombstone**, `Cache-Control: no-store` |
| `/comments/{uuid}` of a LOCAL comment on a public video | AP | 200 AS `Note` |
| `/comments/{uuid}` of a FEDERATED comment | AP | **404** — its id belongs to its origin |

Two of those are worth their own sentence. **404 for a private video is the same
answer as for a uuid that never existed**, so the endpoint cannot be walked to
learn which ids this instance holds. And the **Tombstone carries the id, the
formerType and the deletion time and nothing else** — a retraction that
described what it retracted would defeat the deletion it announces. It is never
cached, because a 410 is the one answer that can legitimately become a 200 again
after a restore.

The ETag is computed over the SERIALISED document rather than a row's
`updated_at`, because the document is what the peer caches: a change to how we
RENDER a video must invalidate it just as a change to the video does.

**The routing half is the operator's**, and it is this repo's diff.
`deploy/Caddyfile` now content-negotiates `/videos/*` and `/comments/*` to the
api on an ActivityPub `Accept` and leaves every other request on the frontend
fallthrough. A browser never matches — Chrome and Safari send
`text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8`, with neither
media type in it — and the api answers 406 anyway, so a mis-fire is a visible
refusal rather than a silently wrong page. **Not exercised against a running
Caddy in this slice**; that belongs to the re-run.

**Signed fetch is NOT implemented and is recorded as a follow-up.** These
objects are public by construction, so nothing here leaks — but a peer that
requires signed dereferencing (Mastodon in secure mode) is not served, and
vidra sends no signature on its own outbound object fetches either.

### The findings, one line each

| id | what A29 measured | this slice |
|---|---|---|
| **A29-F1** | playback and posters do not federate | **fixed** — `icon`, `duration`, HLS `url`; `Update` on transcode completion; CORS on public media |
| **A29-F2** | the AP object id is not dereferenceable | **fixed** — core handlers + the Caddy negotiation rule |
| **A29-F3** | `ResolveSearchTarget` never consults the stored row | **fixed** — the store is consulted first, by object id OR watch url |
| **A29-F4** | a blocked instance's activity is answered 202 with no record; refused activities are never redelivered | **half fixed** — a `federation.inbox.rejected` audit row now exists (the 202 is deliberately unchanged); **redelivery after an unblock is still not attempted** and stays open |
| **A29-F5** | a cancelled `Undo` leaves a ghost follower | **fixed** — an `Undo` or `Reject` bound for a blocked destination is delivered, not cancelled |
| **A29-F6** | the REST follower count excludes remote followers | **fixed** — one definition, local + accepted remote, shared with the AP collection |
| **A29-F7** | no per-remote-account block exists | **fixed** — `remote_actor_blocks` + `/me/blocks/remote` + a settings tab |
| **A29-F8** | a follower instance stores no federated comments | **fixed for the direction A29 measured** — the thread the origin sends is mirrored and shown; AUTHORING against a remote video stays deferred, see below |
| **A29-F9** | a deleted video's AP id answers 200 | **fixed** — 410 + Tombstone |
| **A29-F10** | deliveries carry no correlation id; `/admin/system` has no federation component | **fixed** — identity on the queue row and onto `job_runs`; a `federation` component |
| **A29-F11** | account actor collections are hard-coded empty | **deferred** — a documented decision in `collections.go`, unchanged |
| **A29-F12** | the SSRF guard skips the cached actor; a rotated key is unrecoverable | **fixed** — the guard runs on every resolution; one bounded re-fetch on a verification failure |

### The mirrored thread, and the half of A29-F8 that stays deferred

A29 measured the drop end to end and it was silent on both sides: A's creator
replied to their own video, the reply fanned out as `Create{Note}` to all three
follower inboxes, all three deliveries succeeded — and B stored **zero**
comments. `resolveNoteTarget` requires `inReplyTo` to resolve to a LOCAL video,
so a follower receives every federated comment for the videos it follows and
drops every one, while the sender's ledger records a success.

Migration **0140** gives them somewhere to live: `remote_video_comments`, a
SEPARATE table rather than a nullable `comments.video_id`. `comments` is the
most-joined table in the schema and every moderation, notification,
watched-word and listing query reads that NOT NULL column, so admitting rows
about a video this instance does not host would put a NULL check into all of
them. These rows are also a different KIND of thing — a mirror of somebody
else's thread, with no local author, that only the origin may write.

**The authority rule has three checks and the third is specific to this path.**
The activity's actor is the signer; the Note lives on the signer's origin and is
attributed to it; and **the Note's origin is the VIDEO's origin**. Without the
third, any instance in our follow graph could write onto any mirrored video from
any other instance — the thread would be writable by every peer we follow rather
than by the server that hosts it. Edit and retraction are honoured under the
origin's authority, and a stranger's retraction is refused; a redelivery does not
double the thread.

`GET /api/v1/remote-videos/{id}/comments` is the read, gated on the VIDEO's own
visibility first so the thread cannot be used to probe for a hidden video, and
filtered by the same three controls the card uses (admin instance block for
everyone; the viewer's instance mute and per-remote-account block when signed
in), so a thread can never show what the card would have hidden.

**What stays deferred, and why it is a ruling rather than work: AUTHORING.**
There is no `user_id` column and no POST, deliberately. Writing a comment here
about a video hosted elsewhere reverses a shipped product decision ("comments,
ratings and saving live on the origin instance") and raises a question mirroring
does not — who answers for a comment an instance hosts about a video it does not
own. It would also need an outbound `Create{Note}` addressed to the ORIGIN's
inbox rather than to channel followers, and A29-F11 means an account has no
follower collection to fan out to either. The follower's page now says exactly
this: replying lives on the origin, and the comments shown are a copy of the
origin's thread.

### The per-remote-account block, and what it can honestly promise

`remote_actor_blocks` (migration **0138**) is keyed on the ACTOR URL rather than
a `remote_actors` FK, and both consequences are the point: a viewer can block an
actor this instance has never cached (an actor is NAMED in an activity before it
is ever resolved), and evicting the actor cache cannot silently lift a block.

| | effect |
|---|---|
| the blocker's feeds and reads | that actor's remote videos are excluded — the same `NOT EXISTS` clause the instance-mute already uses, added to all six viewer-facing remote-video queries |
| an inbound `Create{Note}` on a video the BLOCKER owns | dropped, not stored |
| an inbound `Follow` of a channel the BLOCKER owns | records nothing, sends nothing (a `Reject` would tell the blocked actor exactly what happened) |
| another viewer | unaffected — one-directional and per-viewer, like every other viewer control |
| the blocked actor's view of the blocker | **unchanged**, and it cannot be otherwise |
| delivery to the blocked actor's instance | **unchanged**, and it cannot be otherwise |

The last two rows are why this is a block and not a promise: a remote server
decides what it shows its own users, and a safety feature that only READS as
protection is the worst kind.

The surface is `GET`/`POST`/`DELETE /api/v1/me/blocks/remote` — a sibling of
`/me/blocks/{id}` rather than an extension of it, because an actor URL cannot be
a path segment. A handle is resolved through WebFinger (the actor URL for
`user@domain` is whatever that server says it is, so string-building one would
key the block on a URL that never appears in any activity); a URL is validated
and SSRF-guarded but **never dereferenced**, because a block has to work against
an actor that is offline, gone, or refusing us — which is the actor most likely
to be blocked. Unblock matches the stored URL VERBATIM, so a WebFinger that has
since started failing can never strand a viewer with a block they cannot lift.

### Migrations

**0138** `federation_social_parity` — `federated_video_tombstones` (an id and a
time, and nothing else: that is the entire content of a Tombstone) and
`remote_actor_blocks`. **0139** `federation_delivery_identity` —
`request_id`/`correlation_id` on `federation_deliveries`, plus a SECOND trigger
that carries them onto the `job_runs` row the 0083 projection creates. A second
trigger rather than a rewrite of `sync_legacy_job_run()`: that function is
shared by seven legacy queues, and replacing 150 lines of it to add two
assignments would fork a body that must stay identical for every other table.
Row triggers fire in alphabetical order by trigger name, and
`federation_deliveries_operational_projection` sorts before
`federation_deliveries_run_identity`.

**0140** `remote_video_comments` — the mirrored thread (above).

0137 belongs to the A33 purge-jobs slice, which merged during this one; the
branch was rebased onto it and the numbering is contiguous.

Both migrations were **applied to a real PostgreSQL 16.15**, not merely linted:
`migrate up` from an empty database reached version 140 clean, and the
integration suites then ran against that schema.

### The federation component on /admin/system

A29 measured `/admin/system` reporting `ok` across ten components with two
dead-lettered deliveries on the books, because federation had no component at
all. It has one now, and the two failure modes it separates are unrelated:

* **dead letters → `degraded`**, and the overall verdict stays `ok`. A peer
  that will not accept our activities is not this instance being down, and a
  permanently unreachable server would otherwise hold the page red forever.
* **the oldest PENDING delivery older than 20 minutes → `down`.** That is the
  full ladder (30 s doubling to attempt 6 ≈ 15.5 min) plus a drain interval's
  slack, so a queue walking its backoff honestly is never called stalled — only
  one nothing is working on.

The component is **absent**, not `ok`, when federation is not wired: an instance
that does not federate has no federation health, and claiming it is fine would
be a claim about something that is not running. `last_delivered_at` rides along
because a drained queue and a queue nothing is draining look identical by depth.

`vidra-core`: `make ci` **PASS** (fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint — **140** up
migrations clean, openapi-verify, sqlc-verify, test-race). `go vet
-tags=integration ./...` clean. `go test -tags=integration -count=1 -p 1
./internal/federation/... ./internal/store/... ./internal/httpapi/...` **ok** on
a **fresh** PostgreSQL 16.15 created for this slice — separately per package,
because the A29 section's reused-database flake is real: `internal/store`'s
owner-claim test needs an empty `users` table and fails after the federation
suite has seeded one, on this branch and on clean `main` alike.

`vidra-user`: the whole canonical gate — `typecheck`, `lint` (2 pre-existing
warnings, 0 errors), `lint:icons`, `test` (**256 files, 2555 tests**), the
production `build`, and the MOCKED Playwright suite (**627 specs**) — all pass,
**on Node 22 rather than the Node 26 CI uses**, which is what this machine has.
`player-theater.spec.ts` failed once in the full run and passes in isolation:
the known load flake, not a regression. The BACKED Playwright suites were not
run locally.

The mocked suite is also what caught the one real defect in this slice's
frontend half: `e2e/remote-videos.spec.ts` pinned the old info-panel sentence
verbatim, and "comments, ratings, and saving live on the origin instance" became
misleading about READING the moment the page started showing the origin's
thread. The copy and the spec now separate authoring from reading.

This repo: `bash -n` on the touched script (none — only `deploy/Caddyfile` and

### Unverified, and named rather than skipped

**Two-instance re-run pending.** Every claim above is a unit or integration
assertion. Nothing here was measured against a second live instance, a browser,
a caching edge or a running Caddy. What the re-run has to prove, in order:

1. B's remote watch page renders a `<video>` and Chromium reports a decoded
   frame from A's HLS — the whole point, and the only proof that the CORS header
   and the `url` link agree in a real browser.
2. A `Create` sent before A's transcode finished is followed by an `Update` that
   carries the stream link, and B's row gains `stream_url` without a re-Announce.
3. `GET /videos/{uuid}` on A with `Accept: application/activity+json`, THROUGH
   CADDY, returns the AS Video — and the same URL in a browser still returns the
   watch page.
4. Deleting that video makes the same URL answer 410 + Tombstone.
5. Pasting A's video URL into B's search resolves to the row B already holds,
   with no outbound fetch.
6. B's creator blocks one of A's accounts: that actor's videos leave B's feeds,
   its replies stop landing on B's videos, its Follow is refused — and every
   other A account is unaffected.
7. A's `/admin/system` shows a `federation` component, and a delivery's
   `job_runs` row carries the correlation id of the request that queued it.
8. An unfollow issued while the destination is blocked delivers its `Undo`.
9. A peer that rotates its keypair is verifiable again on the next activity.
10. A's creator's reply now APPEARS on B's remote watch page — the exact
    delivery A29 watched succeed into a drop — and A's edit and retraction of it
    follow through.

**Interoperability is still unverified.** The outbound `url` array, the `icon`
Image and the `PT…S` duration follow PeerTube's convention and are read by
vidra's own ingest; no PeerTube or Mastodon instance has seen them.

**Signed fetch on the object routes** is not implemented (recorded above).
**QoE for remote playback is deliberately not emitted** — `useRemotePlayback`
passes no session and no telemetry, because this instance neither brokers nor
delivers those bytes, so A35's truth holds by ABSENCE. No `SourceRemote` was
added to `internal/qoe`'s closed vocabulary: it would be a member no code path
can produce, and a dead vocabulary member is exactly the kind of thing that
later reads as coverage. Whether a viewer's own instance SHOULD measure playback
it did not serve is a product question this slice was not given.

**A29-F4's redelivery half stays open, and so does A29-F8's AUTHORING half** —
both named above, both for reasons stated rather than shaded.
MIG-06's identity/`Move` clause stays deferred, unchanged.

### Found on the way, unrelated to A29

**Six other legacy queues have the identity gap 0139 closes for one.** A17
recorded that federation deliveries carry no correlation id, and this slice
fixed it — but the cause is not specific to federation. `sync_legacy_job_run()`
(migration 0083) projects SEVEN queue tables into `job_runs` and writes no
`request_id`/`correlation_id` for any of them, and 0133's
`inherit_job_run_identity` only fills a CHILD run from its PARENT, so a
top-level projected run has nothing to inherit from. `transcode_jobs`,
`import_jobs`, `caption_jobs`, `account_exports`, `atproto_posts` and
`peertube_import_runs` therefore still show an empty request id on
`/admin/jobs`, under the same advice — "inspect correlated system logs" —
pointing at logs that share no id with the run. Closing it for all seven is one
change (either widen the shared function once, or repeat 0139's sibling-trigger
shape per queue that carries the columns), and it was deliberately not folded in
here: A29's slice should not rewrite a function six other acceptances depend on.

**Echo's CORS middleware stamps `Vary: Origin` on every response**, including
the shared-cacheable ones A33 promoted for the edge. Nothing here changed it and
the public-media header this slice adds is a constant that does not vary by
origin — but it means an edge entry keys on a header the response does not
actually depend on. Worth a look in a delivery slice, not this one.

**The meta repo's `pull_request` CI did not fire for this branch at all.**
`meta-ci` and `ci-required` both ran on `a26/live` and `a33/purge-families`
pull requests and produced no run whatsoever for `a29/remediation`, before or
after the draft was marked ready. `meta-ci` was dispatched manually against the
branch and passes; `ci-required` has no `workflow_dispatch` trigger, so it could
not be. That is a CI-visibility gap of exactly the kind `ci-required` exists to
catch, and it cannot catch its own absence.

## A33 rehearsal — CDN edge simulator against the merged remediation — 2026-09-08

**INT-10 flips to PASS**, with the two deferrals the row has always carried and
one residual it names rather than hides: `PASS (edge simulator; selected edge
deferred; clause 4 residual: no proxy fallback after an edge 5xx)`. This is
slice 3 — the measurement the two remediation sections above deliberately did
not claim. Five of INT-10's six failing clauses were re-run against a caching
edge that holds a copy, and all five are closed; the sixth, clause (4), was
never in either slice's scope and is unchanged, so it is written into the row's
own cell as the residual rather than left to be rediscovered. Complete result:
[`a33-rehearsal.json`](evidence/a33-rehearsal.json); the edge is the same
[`a32-a33-edge-simulator.go`](evidence/a32-a33-edge-simulator.go), re-keyed —
see below.

The lab is A32/A33's shape with the origin moved. A vidra-core api on
127.0.0.1:8088 and a second process at `VIDRA_ROLE=worker`, behind the pipe-only
one-origin proxy on 127.0.0.1:8099 that drops the client's `Accept-Encoding` and
never follows a redirect, in front of `node .next/standalone/server.js` on
:3100; native PostgreSQL 16.15 on 55461 and redis on 56401, both fresh; schema
**140**; frontend the unmodified `main` `766bb59`, rebuilt so
`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8099` is baked; Node 26.8.1; browser
Playwright 1.62.1's real Chromium. The object store is one
`mirror.gcr.io/minio/minio` on 127.0.0.1:9210, bucket `vidra-a33`, **with no
bucket policy applied at all** — which is the first result and not a setup
detail. The edge simulator is on 127.0.0.1:9310 with `-origin
http://127.0.0.1:8088`: the api, not the bucket.

**The run started on `85e4a91` and every number below is `59d7f51`'s.** core
#203 (A29 remediation) landed on `main` mid-run and it touches exactly one thing
this row measures — the CORS header on public media — so the binary was rebuilt
at the new tip, the database migrated 137 → 140, and the whole origin-model
table re-measured rather than re-based by assertion. The pre-#203 reading is
reported where it differs and nowhere else.

Lab deviations, recorded rather than hidden: `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false`;
**`MALWARE_SCAN_MODE=disabled` explicitly**, because there is no clamd on this
machine and core #201 makes every ingestion refuse without one;
`VIDRA_ALLOW_PLAIN_HTTP=true` + `VIDRA_TLS_MODE=plain-http`;
`TRANSCODING_MIN_FREE_SCRATCH_MB=256` against the shipped 10 GiB floor on a box
with 9.8 GiB free, with 6-second 640×360 fixtures to match;
`MEDIA_GC_ENABLED=false` so a superseded generation stays observable, the sweep
then run by hand through `POST /admin/media/gc`; and `REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true`
for the whole run, for two synthetic actors.

**The fixture had to be re-keyed, and that is a finding about the change rather
than about the fixture.** The committed simulator was written for the
key-addressed model and keyed its cache on the request **path**, because a
key-addressed edge URL is `base + "/" + <object key>` and has no query at all.
Against #199's api-as-origin model that is wrong in two ways that both pass
silently: every generation of a segment collapses onto one cache entry (the `?v=`
tag lives in the query, which is the entire point of putting it there), and the
origin fetch drops `__vidra_edge=1`, so the api answers the edge with a redirect
back to the edge — a loop, not a cache. Cache key and origin fetch now both
carry the whole request URI, which is also exactly what `cdn.Provider.Purge`
names. Anyone re-running A32/A33's numbers against current `main` needs this
commit first.

### SC1 — the origin model

The edge URL the api emits is the operator's base plus this api's own media
route path **and query**, plus the marker:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:9310/api/v1/videos/<id>/hls/cmaf/chunk-0-00001.m4s?v=dla1t3y805q0&__vidra_edge=1
```

| route | a viewer, anonymous, direct to the api | the edge's own origin fetch (`__vidra_edge=1`) |
|---|---|---|
| `/hls/master.m3u8?v=`, `/hls/cmaf/media_N.m3u8?v=` | 200 `private, max-age=31536000, immutable` | **never reaches the edge** — not `Redirectable` |
| `/hls/cmaf/media_N.m3u8` (no `?v=`) | 200 `private, max-age=0, must-revalidate` | never reaches the edge |
| `/storyboard.vtt` | 200 `private, max-age=300, must-revalidate` | never reaches the edge |
| `/hls/cmaf/init-N.mp4?v=`, `…/chunk-N-*.m4s?v=` | **307** → edge; the 307 itself `private, max-age=300, must-revalidate` | 200 **`public, max-age=31536000, immutable`**, `video/mp4` |
| `/hls/cmaf/chunk-N-*.m4s` (no `?v=`) | 307 → edge | 200 **`public, max-age=0, must-revalidate`** |
| `/original` | 307 → edge | 200 **`public, max-age=3600, must-revalidate`**, `video/mp4` |
| `/download/original` | 307 → edge | 200 **`public, max-age=3600, must-revalidate`**, `video/mp4`, **`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=fixture.mp4`** |
| `/thumbnail`, `/storyboard.jpg` | 307 → edge | 200 **`public, max-age=300, must-revalidate`**, `image/jpeg` |
| a superseded `?v=` tag | 404 `private, no-store` | 404 `private, no-store`, passed through and **not cached** (MISS on two consecutive tries) |
| `Authorization` present | 200 `private, no-store`, no `Location`, no CORS header | never reaches the edge |

**An edge origin fetch is never answered with a redirect**: across the eight
edge-marked probes the count of `Location` headers is **zero**. Content type and
disposition reach the edge intact, because the edge now fetches the route that
sets them — A32/A33's `application/octet-stream`-with-no-filename result is gone
by construction, not by a backfill.

**Private and unlisted media never get an edge URL, and the bucket stays
private.** On a private video every media route answers 404 to an anonymous
caller with no `Location` ever present, and the edge's own marked fetch is 404
too. An unlisted video is served by the origin at `private` and is **never**
307'd. And an unauthenticated `curl` straight at MinIO answers **403
`AccessDenied`** for `thumbnails/<id>.jpg` and `web-videos/<id>.mp4` alike —
because no bucket policy was applied at any point in this run. That retires
A32/A33's origin-exposure finding by construction: an api-origined edge needs no
public read, so there is nothing for an operator to get wrong there any more.

**Playback.** One Chromium walk of the watch page: **76** requests to the api
origin, **7** to the edge — the poster, the original's 206, both CMAF init
segments and three chunks — 6.014/6.014 s, `readyState` 4, 150 frames, 3
dropped, `error: null`. A second walk answered every one of those seven with
`X-Edge-Cache: HIT`, which is the precondition SC2 needs and the property a
plain reverse proxy could never demonstrate.

**`Vary: Origin`, recorded because the row's neighbour asked for it.** The
shared entry's CORS header **does** vary by the request's `Origin`, measured:
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for an absent or unknown one, and
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://127.0.0.1:8099` **plus
`Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`** for an origin in
`CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`. That is deliberate and written down — `media_cors.go`
says `setMediaCORS` never overwrites a header Echo's CORS middleware already
set, because replacing the allow-listed answer with a wildcard would break every
credentialed media read from the instance's own frontend — and Echo's middleware
supplies the `Vary: Origin` that makes it correct for a compliant cache. The gap
is one level out. `docs/operations.md` tells the operator to forward the query
string *and put it in the cache key*, and then says of the shared entry that
"there is no `Vary` to get wrong": true of the `__vidra_edge=1` marker it is
written about, and **not** true of `Origin`. A CDN that forwards `Origin` and
does not key on it would populate the entry with the allow-listed credentialed
echo on one fetch and hand it to every other origin's player afterwards — which
is precisely the federated playback core #203 exists to enable. The simulator
cannot exhibit it (its cache key is the URL alone and it forwards no `Origin`
upstream at all, so it can only ever hold the `*` variant), and nothing in the
api can enforce a third party's cache key: it is an operator obligation of the
same class as forwarding the query string, and it is the one the operator page
does not state.

### SC2 — a same-source re-transcode, and where the old bytes go

The trigger is `POST /api/v1/admin/videos/{id}/transcoding {"type":"hls"}` →
202 (anonymous **401**, ordinary user **403**), with `transcoding_max_fps` moved
0 → 24 between runs so the encoder genuinely produced different bytes.

| | `videos.transcode_generation` | key prefix | `?v=` | `chunk-0-00001.m4s` sha256 (first 16) | bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | **1** | `streaming-playlists/<id>/r1/` | `dla1t3y805q0` | `a63607893342ca33` | 657,994 |
| after the re-transcode | **2** (bumped at enqueue) | **`streaming-playlists/<id>/r2/`** | `dla1yo2vujsw` | **`60393685106885db`** | **650,072** |
| what the edge served on the NEW url | — | — | `dla1yo2vujsw` | `60393685106885db` (**MISS**) | 650,072 |
| what the edge still holds under the OLD url | — | — | `dla1t3y805q0` | `a63607893342ca33` (HIT) | 657,994 |

The last two rows are the whole result. The old entry is untouched *because it is
a different URL* — nothing was overwritten, so there is no stale-versus-fresh
race to lose. **Zero purge requests** were sent, which is now correct rather
than a gap, and the `same-generation re-transcode overwrites edge-cached objects
without purge` warning appears **zero** times in either process's log: #199
deleted it because the situation it described can no longer arise.

**And the stale segment does not play.** After a reload Chromium issued **0**
requests carrying the old tag and **13** carrying the new one, and decoded
6.014 s at **144 frames** — exactly 24 fps × 6 s, against 150 before. The frame
count is the assertion: the decoder consumed the new generation, not a mixture.

*Mid-playback, honestly.* The fixture is 6 seconds and fully buffered inside the
first second, so a promotion could not be made to land between two segment
fetches; rather than stage a race that would prove nothing, the mechanism was
measured in both directions. A session that already holds the old generation's
URLs finishes off them — the edge keeps serving that entry (HIT) and the objects
stay on disk until media GC. A segment of the old generation the edge does *not*
already hold is refused at the origin with **404 `private, no-store`** the
instant the new generation is promoted — before any sweep — and the edge passes
that 404 through **uncached**. So the answer to "finishes or reloads cleanly" is:
it finishes off what it already has, otherwise it errors, and a reload is clean.

*The old generation's collection.* A dry-run sweep named exactly the **14**
superseded `r1` objects and nothing else; `{"dry_run": false}` deleted 14 of 71
scanned at an orphan ratio of 19 % with the breaker untripped. A subsequent
source replacement (`POST /videos/{id}/replace`) moved the counter 2 → **3**,
which is the readback that matters here — the bucket was not re-listed after
that replacement, so this record claims the counter and not the directory name.

### SC3 — the purge families through the simulator

Every family was measured with the edge **holding a copy first**. The request
`internal/cdn` sends is one `PURGE http://127.0.0.1:9310/<the same URL a viewer
was handed, marker and all>` carrying `X-Edge-Purge-Token`; the simulator
recorded the token as accepted on every call.

| family | trigger → status | purge requests | edge before → after | the durable record |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| poster replacement (multipart) | `POST /videos/{id}/thumbnail` → 201 | **1** (200, held) | HIT `ace182d944f37b22` 18,954 B → **MISS `5a46d2dcf4cf3751` 1,604 B** | immediate pass; `cdn_purge` counters |
| poster replacement (frame pick) | `POST /videos/{id}/thumbnail {"at_seconds":3}` → 201 | **1** (200, held) | evicted | immediate pass |
| storyboard regeneration | `POST /videos/{id}/replace` → 200 | **1** (200, held) on `/storyboard.jpg` | HIT `24d31a9747f9b3e3` 17,087 B → **MISS `c037a57f893a9104` 9,270 B** | immediate pass; the purge named `/storyboard.jpg` and nothing else |
| privacy flip public→private *(control)* | `PATCH /videos/{id}` → 200 | **13** (6×200, 7×404) | that video's 6 entries evicted; the other video's 6 untouched | immediate pass |
| deletion *(control)* | `DELETE /videos/{id}` → 204 | **13** (6×200, 7×404) | emptied | immediate pass |
| account deletion | `DELETE /auth/me` → 204 | **13** (6×200, 7×404) | emptied | one **queued** job `reason=account_delete`, 13 urls, `url_set_complete=t` → `done`, urls emptied |
| instance-wide download revocation | `PATCH /admin/instance-settings {"downloads_enabled": false}` → 200 | **8** (6×200, 2×404) | each video's four download URLs evicted — **`/original` and `/thumbnail` deliberately left in place** | one **leased walk** job, cursor persisted per page → `done`, `purged=8`, `url_set_complete=t` |

The 13-URL takedown set is exactly what slice 1 promised, `?v=` and all:
`/original`, `/download/original`, `/thumbnail`, `/storyboard.jpg`,
`/download/audio`, `/download/hls/360`, `/download/hls/360?audio=false`, and the
six versioned HLS children. The 404s are objects the edge never held, which
`internal/cdn` counts as success. And the download revocation's set being
*narrower* is the visible half of slice 1's "more precise": `/original` survived
the revocation at the edge, so enforcing a download gate no longer cold-starts
every viewer's progressive fallback.

**Resumability.** The catalogue was padded to **252** public downloadable rows
(two real, 250 media-less rows inserted by SQL and sorting after them) so the
walk pages more than once against `DefaultWalkPage = 100`. Page 1 purged all
eight real URLs and persisted `cursor_video_id = f60ad924…`; the worker process
was then killed. **Twenty-five seconds with no worker moved nothing** — cursor,
`purged` and the edge's purge count all frozen, which is the negative control
that makes the next line mean something. The restarted worker resumed **at the
cursor** (`fff8a7b5…`), finished the remaining pages and completed the row, and
the edge's total purge count was **still 8 with no key appearing twice**: the
already-purged videos were not re-issued. Downloads then answer 403 at the api.
A second `downloads_enabled=false` while the walk was live added no second row —
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` against 0137's partial unique index, exercised against a
real planner rather than a fake.

**Wrong actors.** `POST /admin/videos/{id}/transcoding` and `PATCH
/admin/instance-settings` are **401** anonymous and **403** for an ordinary
user. `PATCH /videos/{id}`, `POST /videos/{id}/thumbnail` and `DELETE
/videos/{id}` are **401** anonymous and **404** for a non-owner — the
non-disclosure answer rather than 403. `DELETE /auth/me` with a wrong password
is **403**.

### SC4 — a refused purge, its ladder, and the dead letter

With the edge's purge endpoint answering 500, a poster replacement's immediate
pass failed and left one row: `kind=urls`, `reason=retry`, `attempts=1`, and
`urls = ["/api/v1/videos/<id>/thumbnail"]` — **this api's own route path**, no
purge endpoint, no edge URL, no token, exactly as slice 2 argued it should be.

| attempt | claimed at | outcome | `next_attempt_at` persisted | interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — the immediate pass | 12:01:29 | 500 | 12:02:29 | **+60 s** |
| 2 | 12:02:29 | 500 | 12:04:30 | **+2 min** |
| 3 | 12:04:40 | 500 | 12:08:40 | **+4 min** |
| 4 | 12:08:40 | **200** | — | row `done`, `purged=1`, urls emptied |

The injection was cleared at 12:06:02 and the 12:08:40 attempt landed, so the
"transient failure self-heals" half is measured rather than argued. The rungs
match `internal/cdnpurge`'s `DefaultRetryBase = 1m`, `DefaultRetryMax = 1h`,
`DefaultMaxAttempts = 8` — seven persisted retries, 123 minutes.

**The operator surface while it was failing**, at attempt 3: `GET
/admin/system` → `cdn_purge` `{runs: 6, keys_purged: 29, keys_failed: 1,
pending_retries: 1, oldest_pending_seconds: 273, dead_letters: 0}`, and `vidra
doctor` → `✓ cdn purge backlog: 1 CDN invalidation(s) in flight, none older than
3h0m0s`.

**The dead letter was forced, and this record says how.** There is no
`--max-attempts` knob and no environment variable wired to
`cdnpurge.WithRetry`, so 123 minutes is the only unassisted route to the cap;
`attempts` was set to 7 on the queue row so the next claim was attempt 8. Every
earlier rung above was measured in real time. The transition itself is the
shipped code's: the row went `state=failed`, `attempts=8`, **`urls` kept**
(`["/api/v1/videos/<id>/thumbnail"]`) with `last_error` naming the 500, and the
three surfaces answered together — `cdn_purge` `{keys_failed: 2,
pending_retries: 0, dead_letters: 1}`; the admin jobs page `{queue:
cdn_purge_jobs, pending: 0, running: 0, done: 3, failed: 1}`; and `vidra doctor`

> ⚠ cdn purge backlog: 1 CDN invalidation(s) GAVE UP after the retry cap … The
> edge is still serving media this instance has stopped serving … and nothing
> will try again → invalidate them by hand at the CDN's own console, then check
> `DELIVERY_CDN_PURGE_URL`/`_METHOD`/`_TOKEN`

plus one `ERROR` log line naming the job, the attempt count and the unpurged
count. **There is no `audit_log` action for a CDN purge at all** — the record is
the queue row, the log line and the counters; the *triggers* are audited
(`content.video.delete`, `auth.account.delete`, `admin.instance.update`,
`content.video.transcode`). That is a defensible split and it is written down
here so nobody looks for a purge in the audit log.

### SC5 — failure after the redirect: clause 4, still open by design

With the edge answering 502 for GETs, the api keeps 307ing (`EdgeURL` never
consults the network, by design), hls.js retried **4** distinct segment URLs a
total of **27** times, and the player then fell through to the progressive
`<video src>` on `/original` — which 307s to the same broken edge — and ended on
`readyState 0` with `MEDIA_ELEMENT_ERROR` code 4. **There is no fallback to the
api proxy**, and `origin/main` has not grown one: the resolver's fail-open
discipline covers *building* a source, not a viewer's fetch failing afterwards,
and the api cannot learn about the latter. The only remedy is the
`delivery_cdn_enabled` kill switch, which needs an admin — and which does work:
flipping it off produced **zero** requests to the edge origin and playback
recovered immediately (5.0 s, 120 frames, 0 dropped, `error: null`). This is the
residual the row's new cell names.

### Gates

**No vidra-core, vidra-user or vidra-search file changed** — nothing needed
fixing, which is the point of a rehearsal. Only this repo's docs and the
committed lab fixture. The simulator is `gofmt`-clean and `go build`s; `bash -n`
and `shellcheck` pass on every tracked script; `docker compose -f
docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file <filled> config -q`
passes; `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p '*_test.py'` is **48 tests OK,
zero skips**. Because a MinIO was up, the S3 integration lane was run against it
as well — `S3_TEST_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:9210 go test -tags=integration
./internal/storage/...` is **69 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 SKIP**. `make ci` was **not**
re-run: no vidra-core file changed in this slice, and #199's and #202's own
sections carry their green runs.

### Unverified, and named rather than skipped

The **selected edge** stays deferred — no CDN zone or credential is on this
machine, so every number here is the simulator's. What a real CDN adds is its
own TTL policy, its purge API's rate limits, whether it forwards the query
string and `Origin`, and whether its cache key honours `Vary` — and the last two
are exactly what the CORS note above turns on. The **selected bucket** stays
deferred (MinIO only), though this topology no longer needs a public-read bucket
at all. **Safari/WebKit** was not driven in this slice; A32/A33 measured WebKit
taking the same MSE path and nothing in #199 or #202 touches the client.
vidra-user's `e2e-backed (s3)` lane was not executed (it needs Docker Compose);
no vidra-user file changed. The **dead-letter transition was forced** by writing
`attempts=7` rather than waiting 123 minutes. **Mid-playback across a promotion
was not observed as a race** — see SC2 for what was measured instead. And the
walk's **paging was measured against a padded catalogue**: the cursor, the claim,
the kill/restart and every purge call are the real code; only the row count is
synthetic.

### Findings

1. **All four previously unwired purge families now evict the edge's copy**, and
   the next fetch serves new bytes — poster replacement in both its forms,
   storyboard regeneration, account deletion (queued after the cascade) and the
   instance-wide download revocation (leased, resumable, cursor-persisted).
   F06's ledger is empty and measured empty.
2. **A same-source re-transcode's stale segment no longer plays.** Generation 2
   landed under `r2/` with its own `?v=`, the edge served the new bytes on a
   MISS, and the browser fetched zero old-tag URLs. Clause (1) is closed.
3. **A superseded `?v=` cannot be resurrected through the edge**: the origin
   refuses it 404 `private, no-store` from the moment of promotion, and a
   `no-store` 404 is not cacheable, so the refusal survives the edge.
4. **The bucket needs no public policy.** Unauthenticated reads straight at the
   store are 403 for every media prefix, with no policy applied. A32/A33's
   origin-exposure finding is retired by construction rather than documented
   around.
5. **The shared edge entry's CORS header varies by request `Origin`** — `*` for
   an absent or unknown one, an echoed origin **plus** `Allow-Credentials` for
   one in `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`. The behaviour is deliberate (`media_cors.go`
   refuses to overwrite Echo's allow-listed answer) and `Vary: Origin` is
   present, so a compliant cache is safe. What is missing is the operator
   sentence: `docs/operations.md`'s "there is no `Vary` to get wrong" is written
   about the `__vidra_edge=1` marker and reads as absolute, and it does not tell
   an operator to include `Origin` in the cache key or to stop forwarding it. A
   CDN that forwards `Origin` and ignores `Vary` would hand one origin's
   credentialed echo to every other origin's player — breaking exactly the
   federated playback core #203 added the header for. Bounded follow-up for
   vidra-core's operator docs, adjacent to A29.
6. **No `audit_log` action exists for a CDN purge.** The record is the
   `cdn_purge_jobs` row, one structured log line and the `cdn_purge` counters.
   Defensible, and worth knowing before an incident.
7. **`cdnpurge.WithRetry` is wired to no environment variable**, so an operator
   cannot tune the ladder and a lab cannot reach the cap by configuration. Not a
   defect; a named limit on what an acceptance run can force.
8. **Clause (4) is unchanged and is the row's residual**: an edge 5xx after the
   307 has no fallback to the api proxy, and the only remedy is the
   `delivery_cdn_enabled` kill switch — which was measured working.

The lab was torn down: the MinIO container and its volume, the edge simulator,
the throwaway PostgreSQL cluster and redis, the frontend, proxy and both core
processes, and every lab account and its media. Credentials, raw logs, the media
fixtures and the browser traces stay private under `/tmp/vidra-a33-r3`; nothing
from it is committed.
## Live hardening — termination, viewer count, recording retention, pinned ingest — 2026-09-08

**INT-01 does not move here.** The A26 lab measured one clause of that row's own
procedure as unmet and recorded four postures for a ruling; the owner has ruled,
and this slice builds the four. What it does not do is re-measure INT-01 — that
takes the publisher, the ingest container and the browser back, and it is the
A26 re-run's job. Everything below is **not lab-observed**; three PRs
([core #206](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/206),
[user #200](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/200), this one).
Migration **0141** (schema 140 → 141) and an `api/openapi.yaml` change, so
user #200 carries the contract regen and stays a draft until core merges.
[Sanitized evidence](evidence/live-hardening.json).

**A moderator can end a broadcast, and so, for the first time, can the creator.**
`POST /admin/live/{id}/terminate` takes admin and moderator — the A16 pair every
other content-moderation route takes, because a moderator exists to stop content
and a broadcast was the one kind they could not stop. `POST /live/{id}/end` is
the owner's, and it did not exist in any form: before it, the only ways off the
