air were stopping the encoder — which leaves the row `live` until the ingest's
stop hook or the duration watchdog catches up — and `DELETE`, which takes the
stream and its replay with it.

**The sequence is four steps and the order is load-bearing.** *One:* the session
ends and the reason is stored in **one statement**, not a flip plus an update — a
crash between the two would leave a stream `ended` with no reason,
indistinguishable from an ordinary publisher disconnect, and the creator would be
told nothing, which is the gap. Live HLS 404s the moment the state is not `live`,
the stream leaves every listing, and every playback token outstanding against it
dies with it. *Two:* the **stream key rotates, before the drop**. The RTMP
boundary authenticates a key, not a session; dropping first leaves a window in
which the encoder reconnects on a credential that still works and is back on air
before the rotation lands. *Three:* the publisher is **disconnected**. *Four:*
the **ordinary stop path** publishes the replay — termination never calls
`RunReplay`, because the recording is still open while the publisher holds the
socket and replaying it there would publish a truncated file. The drop closes the
socket, which fires `on_publish_done`, which is the disconnect→replay path A26
measured working.

**The control contract**, added to the shipped `deploy/media/nginx.conf.template`
and reached through a new `LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| drop | `GET <base>/control/drop/publisher?app=live&name=<stream-id>` |
| probe | `GET <base>/stat` |
| auth | `X-Ingest-Secret: <LIVE_INGEST_SECRET>` — the same secret the hooks present in the other direction, so one rotation covers both halves |

Three details are deliberate. `name` is the **stream id and not the key**,
because the on-publish hook has already renamed the session to the id — the raw
credential never has to leave the database to end a broadcast, which is what the
rename was for. `app` is **`live`, the ingest application, never `hls`**:
dropping `hls` would tear down the loopback packaging push and leave the streamer
connected, so the audience would go dark and the publisher would not notice. And
the `if ($http_x_ingest_secret != …) { return 401; }` guard is the rewrite module,
which runs **before** the content phase, so a wrong or absent secret never reaches
`rtmp_control`; the port is not published to the host either, so the secret is a
second layer rather than the only one.

`LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL` is an operator-configured **infrastructure** endpoint,
the same class as `SEARCH_SERVICE_URL` and `IPFS_API_URL`, and it is expected to
be a private compose address — putting it through `internal/urlsafety`'s
public-address guard would reject every correct value. What is guarded is the
part that could be steered: nothing request-derived reaches the URL except two
query parameters, the app is a package constant and the name is a UUID's string
form, both escaped; the base URL's scheme, host and embedded credentials are
validated **at boot**, so a malformed one fails the process rather than one
moderator's click; and redirects are not followed, so a misconfigured proxy's 302
cannot carry the shared secret to a third host. The config validator **refuses a
control URL with no secret** outright — anything that can reach an
unauthenticated control surface can disconnect every publisher on the instance.

**Without a control surface the termination still works, and says what it did
not do.** The response is not a `204`: the three parts fail independently, and a
moderator told only "ok" while the streamer keeps uploading to the operator's
disk has been misinformed at the moment it matters most. `publisher_disconnected`
and `stream_key_rotated` report each, and a `detail` sentence names what survived
— an instance with no `LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL` is told the broadcast is off the
air and the key is dead and the socket is open. The one failure returned as an
**error** rather than a partial result is the state write itself, because it is
the only one that leaves the stream on air; a test asserts that neither the
rotation nor the drop runs after it.

**The audit row carries the stream.** A26 measured every live audit row leaving
`resource_id` empty with the id buried in free-text `reason`, so the audit filter
could not target a stream. `content.live.terminate` puts the id in `resource_id`
and keeps `reason` to the allow-listed **code** — `audit_log` cannot carry prose
(A16) — plus the markers `publisher_not_dropped` / `key_not_rotated` when they
occurred, so a partial outcome is reconstructable a week later. The moderator's
own words live on the `live_streams` row, exactly where a video block's reason
lives, and reach **the creator, their channel managers and staff and nobody
else**: a takedown notice on a public page is a punishment nobody ruled on. The
columns clear on the next go-live, and only then — a terminated permanent stream
allowed to broadcast again must not carry last month's notice forever, and
leaving live is precisely when the creator needs to read it.

The creator sees it on the stream page and in the Studio, from one copy module so
the two cannot drift, and the ended-state branch keys on the termination as well
as on the state because a terminated **permanent** stream returns to `offline`,
not `ended`. Their own end reads *"You ended this stream"* rather than an
accusation. A moderator's End-stream dialog sits on the live watch page, which is
where a moderator watching an instance-damaging broadcast actually is.

**Viewer count, from playlist fetches.** A player refetches the live playlist
about every two seconds for exactly as long as it is watching and stops the
moment it is not, so it is the only request in the live path that means "still
here" — segments would measure bandwidth and `GET /live/{id}` would measure page
views. Viewers are distinguished by a keyed, day-scoped digest under its **own**
domain label, so a live digest and a QoE digest for the same person on the same
day are unrelated values. The client-minted `?s=` session id was the other
candidate and was rejected: a count keyed on a value the client controls is a
count anyone can inflate by rotating a UUID, and a concurrent-viewer number a
viewer can set is worse than none.

The window is **90 seconds** against that ~2 s refresh — deliberately generous,
so a stalled player or a locked phone does not flicker out and back in; the cost
is that the number lags a mass exit by up to 90 s, which is the right way round.
The read is refreshed **at most every 10 seconds**, because the public rail
renders many cards per request and must not pay a round trip per card. Memory is
one Redis sorted set per live stream that prunes on every write and re-arms a
TTL of window + 60 s, so a stream nobody terminates cleanly still evicts itself;
the read counts by range rather than `ZCARD`, so a stale member no write has
pruned cannot inflate the answer. A35's rule is honoured by **counting an
opted-out viewer as the anonymous visitor A13 says they asked to be**, through
the same `searchConsent` predicate the QoE beacon uses — QoE's own empty-digest
answer would be wrong here, because the digest is a set MEMBER and every
opted-out viewer would collapse into one and be under-reported. No Redis, no
count: the field is **omitted rather than zeroed**, because "nobody is watching"
and "I cannot tell" are different statements and only one belongs on a creator's
page mid-broadcast. The frontend guards on `typeof === "number"` and a test pins
that a real measured zero renders.

**720p30 H.264 + AAC-LC** is now stated as the supported publisher profile, in
`vidra-core/docs/operations.md` and on the Studio's Go-live form, because the
ingest transcodes nothing: A26 measured `master.m3u8` carrying zero
`EXT-X-STREAM-INF` lines — it *is* the media playlist — so a creator pushing 4K
has not reached more people, they have made the stream unplayable for everyone
without the bandwidth. Live ABR stays SCP-05.

**`LIVE_RECORDING_RETENTION`.** A26 measured six `.flv` files still on the volume
after one lab session, on a volume the operations doc says is not backed up,
because nothing had ever deleted one. `0` — the default — deletes the recording
as soon as its replay VOD is published: the replay is then the copy, which is
what the recording was an intermediate for. A duration keeps every recording that
long for re-transcoding and the sweep takes it after: hourly, leader-elected,
beside the QoE and audit prunes, in its **own** loop rather than a third pass
inside theirs because it touches a filesystem and a stalled mount must not hold
up the audit trail's retention. **200 files per pass**, oldest first, by mtime and
not by the unix suffix in the name — the suffix is when the recorder *opened* the
file and a long broadcast is still being written hours later.

A **failed replay keeps its recording regardless**: the delete runs only after
the transcode returns successfully, every failure returns early, and the failure
log says the bytes are kept and names the window, because that file is the only
copy that broadcast will ever have. The sweep never touches `rec/.keep`, which is
load-bearing — `record_path` sits inside `hls_path` and the HLS cleanup
`rmdir()`s empty subdirectories of it, which is why replay-to-VOD had never once
run before A26 planted that file. Two gaps at the default are documented rather
than papered over with a hidden floor: a replay-**disabled** stream's recordings
accumulate (the media server records them and no replay is ever published to
trigger the delete) and so does a failed replay's, and a non-zero value is the way
out of both. A sweep that deleted files at a threshold nobody configured is how a
"the only copy" recording disappears.

**The ingest is pinned.**
`alfg/nginx-rtmp:latest@sha256:780831ae1c4116d22a287ce43f9e1befb84ccaad0b6933de041bb29b6427b513`
— the registry's own `docker-content-digest` for the tag, read 2026-09-08, a
single-platform amd64 manifest consistent with A26's note that the lab ran it
under emulation, and a tag that has not moved since 2022, so this is the image
that lab ran. The tag is kept **beside** the digest deliberately: Dependabot's
`docker-compose` ecosystem (already configured at `/`, now annotated to say it
covers this) needs a tag to follow, and a bare `repo@sha256:…` is unbumpable. Meta
pins nothing of its own — `docker-compose.prod.yml`'s `rtmp` block only adds a
restart policy and a log cap on top of core's definition — so there is one pin in
one file.

**A `live_ingest` component** joins the ten on `/admin/system`, and `/readyz` gets
it too (it is on the cheap probe both share). `not_configured` with no
`LIVE_RTMP_URL`, because an install that does no live is not a broken one;
`not_configured` **with an explanation** when live is configured and the control
URL is not, because the finding this component answers is an instance reporting
health it never measured and "ok" would be the same lie in a new place; `ok` when
the stat page answers; `down` when it does not, with a sentence about what it
means for the instance rather than the raw transport error, which names the
ingest's address and travels in screenshots. A dead ingest reads **degraded with
a 200**: only PostgreSQL takes an api out of rotation, and one shared ingest must
never be able to empty every replica out at once. The probe is `/stat` and not a
control command with a dummy name, because a probe that runs on every readiness
tick must have no side effect; it is cached 30 s, so a test asserts 25 readiness
checks cost one round trip.

**Gates.** vidra-core `make ci` — fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint, openapi-verify,
sqlc-verify, test-race — **exit 0**, plus `go vet -tags=integration ./...` exit 0;
29 new tests (20 in `internal/live`, 9 in `internal/httpapi`), and the OpenAPI
contract test caught both new routes as undocumented before the spec was written,
which is what it is for. Three assertions were verified to bite by breaking the
code under them: swapping rotate/drop, skipping the rotation, and a truthy
`viewer_count` guard. vidra-user `npm run ci` on Node 26 — typecheck, lint,
lint:icons, vitest, production build, e2e — **exit 0**: 258 test files / 2579
unit tests and 627 e2e, with 11 added in `LiveWatchView.test.tsx` and 5 in
`lib/live/termination.test.ts`.

That last number was **claimed once before it was true**, and the way it happened
is worth writing down. The vidra-user PR was opened saying `npm run ci` had
passed; it had not — the local run failed `tsc --noEmit` on a session fixture
typed `{ id: string }`, which predates this view reading a role at all, and the
exit code read back was the **background wrapper's** rather than npm's. Five CI
lanes caught it (`frontend`, `ci-required`, both `e2e-backed` variants and
`channel-sync-backed`, every one tracing to the same three type errors), which is
what they are for. The second local attempt then failed on something else
entirely — a fresh worktree has no Playwright browser cache — and only the third
was real. A background job's exit status is the shell's, not the gate's, and a
gate has to print its own. Meta: the Python
suite, the prod compose render `config -q`, the `--profile core --profile
frontend` port assertions and the compose-consumer assert. No script changed.

**Not lab-observed — the A26 re-run is what turns any of this into a
measurement.** No RTMP publisher, no ingest container, no Redis (the viewer
counter is tested against an in-memory store with the same window semantics, not
against a real sorted set), no browser, and no `nginx -t` against the rendered
template — so the `rtmp_control` and `rtmp_stat` blocks have never been parsed by
an nginx, and the drop contract is read off the module's documented behaviour
rather than off the wire. The re-run must prove, in order of how much rests on
it: that a real publisher is actually **disconnected** by a termination (ffmpeg
exits, the ingest logs the drop, zero further bytes reach `LIVE_HLS_ROOT`); that
`nginx -t` accepts the template and that the pinned image's build has the control
and stat modules compiled in at all — if it does not, `/control` answers 404 and
every termination silently degrades; that the 401 gate fires on a missing and a
wrong secret; that terminate → drop → `on_publish_done` → replay yields a
**complete** replay rather than a truncated one; that a rotated key is refused at
the real ingest on reconnect; that two concurrent Chromium viewers read 2 and one
leaving decays to 1 inside the window against a real Redis; that `live_ingest`
flips `ok` → `down` when the container stops while `/readyz` still answers 200;
that retention `0` deletes a real `.flv` after a real replay publishes; and that
the pinned digest is what the `media` profile actually pulls.

**Left alone, deliberately.** `content.live.replay` and `content.live.force_close`
still leave `resource_id` empty — changing an existing action's shape is a
question for whoever consumes the trail, not a hardening one. A hook-only flip
still advertises a byte-less stream on the public rail, nothing resyncs a drifted
player to the live edge, there is still no live ABR ladder, and live streams still
have no server-generated poster.

## CDN follow-ups — edge CORS constancy, retry knobs, purge audit, redelivery after unblock — 2026-09-08

**No register row is re-scored.** INT-10 keeps the PASS and the residual the
rehearsal above gave it, and FED-02 keeps what A29 left it. This slice is the
four defects those two re-runs of the same day RECORDED and did not fix — A33
rehearsal findings 5, 6 and 7, and A29-F4's open outbound half — closed in code
and proven by tests. It is **code-only and deliberately not lab-observed**:
another executor holds the lab, so every claim below is a unit or integration
test, a rendered config, or an explicit statement that something was not
measured. Complete result:
[`cdn-follow-ups.json`](evidence/cdn-follow-ups.json); vidra-core #207, this
repo #156.

### The edge's CORS answer is now a constant

**What failed first.** The rehearsal measured the shared edge cache entry
carrying `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for an absent or unknown `Origin` and
`http://127.0.0.1:8099` **plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`** for
one on the operator's allow-list. Echo's `Vary: Origin` makes that correct for a
compliant cache, and the finding said so — but the entry is ONE object served to
every viewer behind the edge, and a CDN that forwards `Origin` upstream while
ignoring `Vary` would fill it with the operator frontend's credentialed echo and
hand that to every other origin's player. That is precisely the federated
playback core #203 added the header for, and it would break for everyone at
once rather than for the viewer who caused it.

**What changed.** The api stops depending on a third party's cache key. A
request carrying the edge marker to a public media route now **skips echo's CORS
middleware entirely** (`CORSConfig.Skipper = Server.edgeMediaRequest`), so the
answer is the constant wildcard `setMediaCORS` writes, with no
`Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` and **no `Vary: Origin`**, whatever `Origin`
arrived. Nothing is lost: the edge is only ever handed public, non-credentialed
bytes, and a credential cannot be used with a wildcard origin anyway.

The mechanism is the skipper rather than a strip after the fact, and that is the
whole choice. A strip would have to run in every handler that answers a media
route and would silently do nothing in the one that forgot to call it; skipping
is a property of the ROUTE plus the marker, so it holds for every response on
that request — error responses and any media handler added later included.
`mediaPreflight` consequently answers an edge-marked `OPTIONS` itself (204 and
the same constant), because the middleware that used to terminate it is the one
being skipped and a GET-only route would otherwise answer 405, which a browser
reads as a refused cross-origin fetch. A CDN with the api as origin forwards a
browser's preflight upstream, marker and all, so that is a real path.

**A viewer's request is untouched**, and there is a test that says so rather
than a comment: the same media route without the marker, and a JSON route with
it, still get the allow-listed origin, `Allow-Credentials: true` and
`Vary: Origin`. Without that assertion a green suite would be equally consistent
with "CORS was turned off". With the skipper removed, the positive test fails on
five assertions — `Vary: [Origin]` for all three origins and the credentialed
echo for the allow-listed one — which is the rehearsal's measurement reproduced
in a unit test.

`docs/operations.md` is corrected in the same commit. The CDN expectations list
gains **"do not key on `Origin`"** (forwarding it is harmless; keying on it only
fragments the cache), and the sentence the finding named — "there is no `Vary`
to get wrong", true of the `__vidra_edge=1` marker it was written about and
absolute as it read — is replaced by a section stating the guarantee, why the
api makes it itself instead of asking an operator to configure a cache key, and
that a viewer's own answer is unchanged.

### The purge retry ladder is configurable

`cdnpurge.WithRetry` was wired to no environment variable, so an operator could
not tune what their instance does when its CDN stops accepting invalidations,
and the rehearsal could only reach the dead-letter cap by writing `attempts=7`
into a queue row by hand — 123 minutes was the only unassisted route.
`CDN_PURGE_RETRY_BASE` (**1m**), `CDN_PURGE_RETRY_MAX` (**1h**) and
`CDN_PURGE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (**8**) now feed it, with the defaults equal to the
package's own constants and a test that keeps them equal.

Validation refuses a non-positive base or cap, a **cap below the base** (which
would clamp every retry to the cap and remove the backoff entirely — a ladder
with no rungs, not a slower one) and fewer than one attempt (attempt 1 IS the
immediate pass, so 1 is legal and 0 would dead-letter work never attempted).
All of it is checked on every config, CDN or not: unlike a purge URL or token
these have working defaults, so an inert value is not the "configured the half
you thought mattered" bug — but a nonsense value is still a lie about what the
instance will do in an incident.

They reach both `api` and `worker` through vidra-core's shared compose anchor,
and are documented in `.env.example` (with the lab recipe —
`CDN_PURGE_RETRY_BASE=1s CDN_PURGE_MAX_ATTEMPTS=2` dead-letters in seconds) and
in this repo's `env/production.env.example`, which states what a dead letter
MEANS rather than only what the numbers are. The compose values are pinned to
the shipped defaults rather than left empty, which does shadow the Go defaults
in A17's sense: they are safe to pin because a test keeps the two equal, and an
empty value would leave the ladder invisible in the rendered model an operator
inspects.

### A purge job's outcome is in the audit trail

Finding 6 was that **no `audit_log` action for a CDN purge existed at all**: the
whole durable record of a takedown reaching, or failing to reach, the edge was a
`cdn_purge_jobs` row that a retention sweep eventually deletes, one structured
log line, and a process-local counter a restart resets.

`cdn.purge.completed` and `cdn.purge.dead_lettered` are now written once per
**job outcome**, actor kind `system`, `job_id` naming the queue row, with
`reason_code`, `url_count`, `purged`, `failed` and `attempts` as allow-listed
metadata. Counts, never URLs: a purge path is built from an operator-supplied
template that can carry a credential, which is why `media_purge.go` refuses to
log one either.

Outcomes only, and queue jobs only. **A scheduled retry writes nothing** —
seven rungs per job would make one flapping edge the bulk of a quiet instance's
security trail, and `attempts`/`next_attempt_at`/`last_error` are already on the
row the admin jobs page renders. The immediate in-request pass writes nothing
either: it is reported by its own audited act (`content.video.delete`,
`auth.account.delete`, `admin.instance.update`, `content.video.transcode`). What
had no record at all is the half that finishes minutes or hours later, in
another process, after that act returned 204 — and, for a dead letter, the fact
that it never finished.

The seam takes the audit **envelope** rather than a bag of scalars, so the test
drives a real `audit.Service` over a fake repository: an unallowed metadata key
or a malformed action is refused by the validator, and that refusal is a test
failure rather than a row that silently never appears in production.

### A29-F4: the outbound half is resumed on unblock

**How cancellation is recorded, established rather than assumed.**
`DrainDeliveries` hands a delivery whose destination is blocked to
`FailDelivery` with `last_error = "cancelled: destination instance is blocked"`.
The row is dead-lettered, **not deleted** — `state='failed'` with `inbox_url`,
`payload`, the signing actor and `updated_at` all intact. So the rows are
retained and the residual this slice was told to record instead does not apply.

A block is symmetric in effect and asymmetric in recoverability. The inbound
half stays unrepairable and this does not pretend otherwise: activities from the
blocked instance were answered 202 and dropped, so the remote considers them
delivered and will never resend. The outbound half is still sitting in the
queue, and leaving it there means a remote follower silently misses every video
published during the block, forever, with no reconciliation path — the same
shape of permanent divergence A29-F5 closed for severing activities.

`UnblockInstance` is now `DELETE … RETURNING created_at`, so the admin who lifts
the block gets the moment it began and the resumption is bounded to that window.
From the DELETE rather than a read before it, so two simultaneous unblocks
produce one window belonging to one of them; the call stays idempotent, with an
unblock of a domain that was not blocked reported as a success with no window.

What is resumed: **Delete** and **Accept** always — the first can only reduce
what the remote holds, the second strands a granted follow if dropped.
**Create** and **Update** only if the activity's object is one of this
instance's own videos (id prefix, not a suffix match) and that video still
exists, is still public and published, and its channel still has ActivityPub
enabled — the payload is a snapshot taken when the activity was queued, and a
video that went private must not be published to a remote server by a message
the block happened to delay. Everything else stays cancelled: `Undo` and
`Reject` were never cancelled in the first place, and an unrecognised type is
not something to replay on a guess. A resumed row goes back to `pending` with
`attempts=0`, because a cancellation was never an attempt on the remote side and
carrying the count forward would dead-letter it early for reasons that have
nothing to do with the destination's health.

The work is capped at 500 rows and detached from the request, for the same
reason the edge-purge fan-out is: an admin's DELETE must not become an unbounded
scan-and-update, and a resumption that did not happen leaves rows exactly where
they already were. The query prefilters on the domain so that cap is spent on
**this** domain's rows — found in review, and silent without it: an instance
with several blocked domains and more than the cap of cancellations in the
window would unblock one and resume none of its deliveries, because the page
came back full of the ones still blocked. The prefilter is not the answer
(`hostOf` still decides, so the two cannot disagree about what host an inbox URL
has); it can only widen the candidate set, never narrow it. The cancel marker is now one constant used by both the drain
that writes it and the query that matches it, and the test drives the
cancellation through the real drain — a test that spelled the string twice would
pass while the two drifted apart.

### Gates

vidra-core `make ci` **PASS** (fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint, openapi-verify,
sqlc-verify, test-race over the whole tree) and `go vet -tags=integration ./...`
clean. **OpenAPI is unchanged**, which openapi-verify asserts, so no vidra-user
regeneration is owed; sqlc v1.31.1 — the pinned version — regenerated the three
query changes and `sqlc-verify` is clean. **No migration**: the cancelled
deliveries were already retained, so core stays at schema 140. In this repo,
`python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p '*_test.py'` is **48 tests OK, zero
skips**; `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml
--env-file <filled> config -q` passes with the eight `${VAR:?}` keys filled with
obvious dummies, and the `--profile core --profile frontend` render shows the
three new knobs on the api service. The meta-ci "every config key vidra-core
reads has a compose consumer" step was re-run locally: **OK, 173 keys, api and
worker maps equal**. No script in either repo was touched, so no `shellcheck`
was owed.

### Not lab-observed, and named rather than skipped

**Nothing in this slice was measured against a running system.** No caching edge:
the constant header set is asserted in-process against the real echo stack, not
through a CDN, so what a real CDN does with a constant answer is unchanged and
remains INT-10's standing selected-edge deferral. No PostgreSQL: the purge audit
row is produced by the shipped `audit.Service` over a fake repository and
validated by the real envelope validator, but no row was written to a real
`audit_log` and no admin audit-log page was read. No second instance: the block,
the cancellation and the resumption run in-process against the fake repository
with the real drain doing the cancelling, so "the remote receives the resumed
Create" is **not** claimed. The retry ladder's rungs were measured in real time
by the rehearsal above and are not re-measured; what is new and unobserved is
that a CONFIGURED ladder is the one the queue uses, which is unit-proven and
rendered-config-proven only. vidra-user and vidra-search are untouched, so
neither suite was run.

### Found on the way, unrelated

**`federation_deliveries` has no retention sweep of any kind.** Nothing in the
tree deletes a delivered row, so every fan-out since the instance was installed
is still in the table — and there is no index for the redelivery query's
predicate either, which makes that scan a sequential one on a long-lived
instance. It is bounded, detached and runs once per unblock, so it is not a
request-latency risk; an index or a sweep is a separate change and is recorded
here rather than folded in.

**`internal/config`'s `DeliveryCDNBaseURL` comment still described the old
topology** — "THE CDN'S ORIGIN MUST BE KEY-ADDRESSED … pointing this at the
Vidra API origin 404s every request" — which #199 inverted three sections ago.
Corrected in passing, since the same struct block was being edited for the
retry knobs.

## A29 rehearsal — two instances against the merged remediation — 2026-09-08

**INT-05 does NOT flip.** Nine of the ten clauses the remediation section listed
for this re-run pass on two live instances, through a real Caddy, in a real
Chromium — including the one that was the whole point: a remote video plays,
with decoded frames counted. The tenth fails, and it fails because the
remediation broke it. INT-05's own procedure says a private or unlisted video
produces ZERO federation activities and A29 measured exactly that; the
transcode-completion hook the remediation added now makes every private and
unlisted upload broadcast a `Delete` naming its uuid to every remote follower.
That is fixed on [vidra-core #209](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/209)
and unmerged as this is written, so the row stays FAIL and names the clause.
Two further sub-clauses of the row's own procedure are unmet and named below.
Complete result: [`a29-rehearsal.json`](evidence/a29-rehearsal.json).

The lab is A29's shape with the edge added. Two isolated instances at schema
**140**, each an api plus a `VIDRA_ROLE=worker` process with its own database,
Redis index, `STORAGE_LOCAL_ROOT` and origin, federating over plain HTTP with
`FEDERATION_ENABLED=true` and a sealed actor KEK on both. `vidra-core`
origin/main **59d7f51** (#203) for everything up to the private/unlisted clause,
then **48374d8** (#209) for that clause's re-measurement and everything after
it — the text says which reading is which. `vidra-user` origin/main **eb99808**
(#198), one `next build`, both frontends the same standalone bundle on Node
26.8.1 with different `INTERNAL_API_BASE_URL`/`PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL`. PostgreSQL
16.15 and Redis 8.6.2 in throwaway instances; ffmpeg 8.1 six-second 640×360
fixtures; Playwright 1.62.1's real Chromium. Two `a29-ap-peer.go` instances —
`commenter` on `:48080` for every input a Vidra instance cannot produce, and
`rotator` on `:58080` for the key-rotation clause.

**The edge is the point of this run, so it is a real one.** Caddy v2.11.4 from
brew, one config with two site blocks that mirror `deploy/Caddyfile` sections 1,
2, 3, **3a** and 4 verbatim in structure: the `/metrics` and `/api/v1/dev/*`
404s, the `@api` path list, the `@ap_object` / `@ap_object_ld` `Accept` matchers
sitting **above** the frontend fallthrough, and `encode zstd gzip` scoped to the
frontend block alone. Only the site addresses and upstreams differ — loopback
ports instead of a domain and compose service names — and `auto_https off` keeps
it plain HTTP, so no internal CA had to be minted or trusted anywhere.
`caddy validate` passed before every start. Section 3a was written by the
remediation and never executed; it is executed now, and it is correct.

Lab deviations, recorded rather than hidden: **`MALWARE_SCAN_MODE=disabled`
explicitly**, because there is no clamd on this machine and vidra-core #201
makes every ingestion refuse without one — `/admin/system` reports it as
`clamav: not_configured` with the whole consequence spelled out, which is the
honest shape; `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false`; `HTTP_IMPORT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_URLS=true`,
the only knob that lets `urlsafety.Guard` reach a loopback origin;
**`VIDRA_ENV=development`**, because production refuses both of those variables
outright and requires an https `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`; `MEDIA_GC_ENABLED=false` and
`TRANSCODING_MIN_FREE_SCRATCH_MB=256` on a box with 9.2 GiB free;
`REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true` throughout, for four synthetic actors. Every KEK is
base64 of 32 identical bytes and every secret is an obviously fake lab string;
none is committed.

### SC1 — the video plays, and the numbers say so

B's `/remote/{id}` renders a real `<video>` and Chromium decodes A's HLS:

| | Create-before-ladder video | publish-after-transcode video |
|---|---|---|
| `readyState` | 4 | 4 |
| `currentTime` / `duration` | 5.783 / 6.014 | 5.787 / 6.014 |
| `videoWidth` × `videoHeight` | 640 × 360 | 640 × 360 |
| `totalVideoFrames` | **143** | **143** |
| `droppedVideoFrames` | 0 | 0 |
| `video.error` | null | null |

Eight responses from A's origin per playback — `hls/master.m3u8`, two CMAF
variant playlists, two `init-*.mp4`, three `chunk-*.m4s` — **all 200, all
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`**, zero `requestfailed` events, zero CORS
console errors, zero page errors. The one console error in the whole walk is an
anonymous `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` answering 422, which is B's own session
probe. The `OPTIONS` preflight hls.js needs for its `Range` fetches answers 204
through Caddy with `Allow-Methods: GET, HEAD`, `Allow-Headers: Range` and
`Max-Age: 600`. The page shows the poster (from B's own
`/api/v1/remote-videos/{id}/thumbnail` — B mirrors the origin's `icon` into
`remote-thumbnails/*.jpg` rather than hotlinking it), the duration as `0:06`,
the `From 127.0.0.1:18080 · ActivityPub` badge, and the
`Watch on 127.0.0.1:18080` link.

**Both orderings were run and they differ exactly as designed.** A video
published before its ladder existed emitted a `Create` carrying only the
`text/html` `/v/{code}` link, then an `Update` carrying
`[application/x-mpegURL master.m3u8, text/html]`; B's row gained `stream_url`
from the `Update` with no re-Announce. A `publish_after_transcode` video's
`Create` ALREADY carried the HLS link, because `releaseHold` publishes first and
`AnnounceVideo` then reads a video that is already public with a ready ladder —
`composeTranscodeCompletion`'s `[release, mirror, federate]` order is what makes
that true, and this is the first time it has been observed rather than asserted.
Both `Create`s also carried `duration: PT6S` and an `icon`, because ffprobe and
the poster both precede the ladder.

**And then the clause that fails.** A PRIVATE upload and an UNLISTED upload,
both reaching `published` with a real HLS ladder, each fanned a
`Delete{http://A/videos/<uuid>}` to **both** remote follower inboxes when their
transcode completed; a `PATCH` of a private video's title fanned two more. A29
measured ZERO activities for precisely this. The cause is two-layered and only
the first layer is new: the transcode-completion hook calls
`federation.UpdateVideo` unconditionally, and `UpdateVideo`'s else-branch
retracts anything that is not public+published — which is also what
`video.WithUpdateHook` has always done, so the metadata-edit half is older than
the remediation and was simply never measured. Neither `Delete` retracts
anything, because the video was never public and no peer ever held it. What it
does do is tell every follower instance the uuid of a hidden video and the
moment it was uploaded.

vidra-core #209 separates the two facts that were being conflated: "not
public+published" and "was WITHDRAWN from public+published". `WithUpdateHook`
now passes whether the video was public+published before the change — the same
shape `WithDeleteHook` already uses for `wasPublic` — and `UpdateVideo` takes
the retraction arm only when it is true; the transcode path passes `false`,
because finishing a transcode never withdraws a video from public. Re-measured
on that binary: a private upload, an unlisted upload and a metadata edit on a
private video produce **zero** deliveries, with all six transcode jobs
`state=done` so the hook really ran; a public video's edit still fans out an
`Update` that lands on B; and flipping a public video to private still fans out
a `Delete` that removes B's row.

### SC2 — the negotiation table, measured through Caddy

| request | Accept | through | answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `application/activity+json` | Caddy | 200 AS `Video`, `public, max-age=300`, ETag |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `application/ld+json; profile="…activitystreams"` | Caddy | 200, byte-identical, same ETag |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | same + `If-None-Match` | Caddy | **304** |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | a real browser's `text/html,…,*/*;q=0.8` | Caddy | 200 the watch page |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `*/*` | Caddy | 200 the watch page |
| `/videos/{uuid}` | `*/*` or `text/html` | the api directly | **406** |
| `/videos/{uuid}` private / unlisted / never-existed | AP | Caddy | **404**, all three identical |
| `/videos/{uuid}` deleted | AP | Caddy | **410 + Tombstone**, `no-store` |
| `/comments/{uuid}` local, on a public video | AP | Caddy | 200 AS `Note`, `public, max-age=300` |
| `/comments/{uuid}` federated | AP | Caddy | **404** |
| `/comments/{uuid}` | `text/html` | Caddy | 404 (frontend has no such route) |

Two things are worth saying out loud. **`*/*` falls through to the frontend**,
so the api's 406 is reachable only by addressing the api directly — Caddy's
matcher needs the literal media type in `Accept`, which is exactly the behaviour
that keeps browsers on the page, but it means the 406 the remediation documents
is an origin-level answer and not an edge-level one. And the Tombstone is
minimal as promised — `id`, `formerType`, `deleted`, nothing else — though it
still carries an ETag, which is meaningless on a 410 and worth deleting the next
time that handler is opened.

**Remote-URL lookup.** B's search resolved A's AP object id and A's `/v/{code}`
watch URL to the SAME already-stored row, B's `remote_videos` count stayed at 2,
and A's request log recorded **no request at all** in that window. The store is
consulted before the network and a pasted URL creates no duplicate.

### SC3 — the block matrix, and the F4 answer

| case | measured |
|---|---|
| inbound `Follow` from B while B's instance is blocked | refused; `remote_follows` unchanged; **audit row `federation.inbox.rejected`** written with `domain=federation`, `reason=domain=127.0.0.1:28080` and the request/correlation ids |
| outbound to B while blocked | cancelled — `state=failed`, `attempts=1`, `last_error: cancelled: destination instance is blocked` |
| unblock, then a NEW activity | delivered; the post-unblock comment reached B's mirrored thread |
| **F4's open half — redelivery after the unblock** | **not redelivered, and worse.** The cancelled rows stay `failed attempts=1` forever, and the inbound `Follow` refused during the block is never re-applied either: A still holds two followers and **B's own row stays `pending` with no retry from B's side**. Neither end re-attempts, so a block taken and lifted leaves the follower's UI showing a follow request that will never resolve. |
| unblock with a percent-encoded domain | `…/blocked/127.0.0.1%3A28080` → **422 invalid domain**; the raw colon → 204 |
| per-account block, handle that does NOT collide | **works** — `films@127.0.0.1:18080` resolved to `/video-channels/films`, that channel's video left the blocker's `scope=all` feed (2 → 1), every other A actor stayed, and anonymous and `otherb` both still saw all four |
| per-account block, handle that DOES collide | **hides nothing** — see below |
| blocked actor's inbound `Create{Note}` | dropped, not stored (202); A's comment count unchanged |
| blocked actor's inbound `Follow` | records nothing, sends nothing (202) |
| blocked actor's EXISTING comment | **still visible** on the blocker's own video, to the blocker |
| `GET /remote-videos/{id}` by the blocker | 200 — the block is scoped to the six listing queries and the mirrored thread, not to a by-id read of a URL the viewer already holds |
| other viewers and anonymous | unaffected throughout |

**The collision, which is the finding.** `federation.WebFinger` resolves a
`name@domain` to the USER first and only then to a channel. On an instance where
a creator's account and their channel share a handle — which nothing prevents;
creating a channel with handle `ownera` while a user `ownera` exists answers
**201** — every channel-scoped federation feature keyed on that handle addresses
the wrong actor, silently. `POST /me/remote-follows` with the handle queues a
`Follow` of a `Person`, which `handleFollow` drops with no record and no
`Reject`, so the follower's row sits `pending` forever. `POST /me/blocks/remote`
with the handle stores `/accounts/<name>` while `remote_videos.remote_actor_url`
is `/video-channels/<name>`, so the blocker's feed does not change. Blocking the
channel actor URL explicitly works (3 → 1) — but the settings page is
placeholdered `@name@instance.example`, and the `RemoteVideo` view the watch page
renders carries `domain`, `object_url` and `watch_url` and **no actor URL and no
channel handle at all**, so there is nowhere for a viewer to copy the identity
that would work. The block a viewer can actually make is the one that does
nothing. This
needs a ruling, not a patch: either the handle namespaces are unified at channel
creation, or WebFinger answers with both links, or the block resolves an
account's channels as well.

**Two more sub-clauses of the row's procedure are unmet.** A blocked remote
account's already-stored comments are not hidden — the remediation's own table
only ever promised that the actor's remote VIDEOS leave six viewer-facing
queries — and no audit row is written for a `Note` or `Follow` dropped by a
per-account block. The second is a defensible recorded decision (a per-viewer
control writing an audit row per dropped activity would be a spam amplifier);
the first is a gap against the settings page's own promise that "their replies
stay off your videos".

**The rest of SC3 passes cleanly.** `otherb`'s unfollow delivered its `Undo`,
A's row was gone within 15 s, `follower_count` went 2 → 1, and the next fan-out
went to `viewerb`'s inbox only — `otherb`'s delivery count frozen at 19 while
`viewerb`'s advanced to 20 (A29-F5). A's REST `follower_count` read **2** with
`channel_follows` empty, identical to the AP collection's `totalItems` — A29
measured 3 vs 0 (A29-F6). The 24 `federation_deliveries` `job_runs` rows
inspected all agreed with their delivery row on `request_id`/`correlation_id`;
the rows that are empty are empty on BOTH sides, because they are the deliveries
queued from the WORKER process where no HTTP request is in scope — the
projection is faithful, but `/admin/jobs` still shows an empty request id for
every worker-queued federation delivery, which is A17's complaint about six
other queues arriving here by a different road. `/admin/system` carries the
`federation` component, reading `degraded` on the two block-window dead letters
while the overall verdict stays `ok` — exactly the separation the remediation
designed. Its
`LastDeliveredAt` is computed in `cmd/api` and never rendered into any response,
so the number that was added to tell a drained queue from an abandoned one is
not actually visible to an operator.

### SC4 — the comment timeline

| time | event | result |
|---|---|---|
| 12:52:58 | signed `Create{Note}` from `commenter@:48080`, `inReplyTo` A's video object url | 202 → stored on A, `remote:true`, `author_username commenter`, `author_id null` |
| 12:53:56 | A's creator posts a top-level comment | `Create{Note}` to both inboxes, both delivered → **B mirrors it** and renders "Comments from the origin · studioa · From 127.0.0.1:18080" |
| 12:53:56 | A's creator replies to the remote commenter's note | both deliveries succeed, **B stores nothing** |
| 12:55 | A's creator replies to its own top-level comment | both deliveries succeed, **B stores nothing** |
| 12:56 | A edits the top-level comment | B's row updated in place, rendered "· edited" |
| 12:57 | `Delete{Note}` for A's comment signed by the unrelated peer | 202, B's row survives — a stranger's retraction is refused |
| 12:58 | A deletes the comment | B's row gone, `GET /remote-videos/{id}/comments` total 0 |
| 13:16 | A deletes the video | B's `remote_videos` row gone and its three mirrored comments with it |

The second row is the clause: **the exact delivery A29 watched succeed into a
drop now lands, and a browser sees it.** The two "stores nothing" rows are new
information the remediation did not state: `storeRemoteVideoNote` resolves the
thread with `GetRemoteVideoByURL(inReplyTo)`, so **only** a Note whose
`inReplyTo` is the video's object url is mirrored. Every reply — to a local
comment or to a remote one — is delivered successfully and dropped silently,
which is the same failure shape A29 found, one level down. In vidra's model
"replying to a video" IS a top-level comment, so the clause the row names is
met and a thread with any depth is not. `remote_video_comments` has no parent
column, so threading is a design change rather than a patch.

Authoring stays deferred, and the page now says so in its own words: "Ratings
and saving live on the origin instance, and so does replying — the comments
below are a copy of the origin's thread, sent here."

### SC5 — signatures, outage, retry

Unsigned, tampered and stolen-`keyId` activities are all **401 signature
verification failed** on both inboxes; a spoofed actor (correctly signed by the
peer, `actor` claiming one of B's accounts) is **400 invalid activity**; A's
comment count was unchanged after all five.

The ladder is unchanged since A29. With B's Caddy site removed so port 28080
refuses connections — a real outage, not a 503 — a comment queued at 13:06:39
was at `attempts=3, next_attempt_at 13:10:37` when read at 13:10:06 and at
`attempts=4, next 13:14:47` when read at 13:11:19: attempt 4 ran at 13:10:47 and
scheduled **+240 s**, the fourth rung of 30 → 60 → 120 → 240. B was restored at
13:11:32 and the delivery went `delivered` at 13:14:57 with `attempts=4`. B
holds exactly **one** copy of it.

**Key rotation (clause 9).** The `rotator` peer's key was cached by A
(`md5 84e8b557…`); the peer restarted with a fresh keypair (`md5 1be52bd3…`) and
sent an activity signed with the new key. A answered 202, refreshed the cached
`public_key_pem` to the new fingerprint, and APPLIED the activity — the `Undo`
removed the follow. One bounded re-fetch on a verification failure, A29-F12
confirmed live.

### Gates

`vidra-core`: `make ci` **PASS** (fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint — 140 up
migrations clean, openapi-verify, sqlc-verify, test-race). `go vet
-tags=integration ./...` clean. `go test -tags=integration -count=1 -p 1
./internal/federation/... ./internal/video/... ./internal/httpapi/...
./cmd/api/...` all **ok** against a fresh PostgreSQL 16.15 migrated to 140. No
OpenAPI change and no migration, so no contract regen was needed and
`vidra-user` was not modified or re-gated.

This repo: `caddy validate` on the lab config; `deploy/Caddyfile` itself is
unchanged — the run reproduced §3a rather than editing it, which is the point.

### Unverified, and named rather than skipped

**MIG-06's identity clause stays unverified**, unchanged and deliberately not
faked: source identity after a migration needs actor-`id` continuity, key
continuity or a `Move`, and `dispatchActivity` still has no arm for `Move`.
**Interoperability** with PeerTube or Mastodon is still unverified — no
third-party server has seen the `url` array, the `icon` Image or the `PT…S`
duration. **TLS and real hostnames** are still unverified: the fediverse domains
here are `host:port` literals, and `/etc/hosts` needs root. **Signed fetch** on
the object routes is still not implemented. The `vidra-user` backed Playwright
suites were not run.

### What would flip INT-05

Merging vidra-core #209 closes the private/unlisted clause, which is the only
one of the ten that fails. The two remaining sub-clauses of the row's own
procedure — a blocked remote account's existing content hidden for the blocking
scope, and the handle/actor collision that makes the block address the wrong
actor — need a ruling or a fix before the row can honestly read PASS, because
they are the same clause (2) the original verdict named. Everything else in
INT-05's procedure has now been measured twice and holds.

## A26 rehearsal — live termination against the merged hardening — 2026-09-08

**INT-01 moves from FAIL to PASS**, and it takes three defects with it. The
hardening slice ("Live hardening — termination, viewer count, recording
retention, pinned ingest") built the moderator's End-stream control and said in
its own words that none of it was lab-observed. This re-run put the pinned
ingest, a real `ffmpeg` publisher and a real moderator in Chromium back in front
of it and found that **the control did not work at all — in three independent
places at once**. Two PRs fix them
([core #211](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/211),
[user #201](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/201)); no migration
(core stays at schema 141), `api/openapi.yaml` unchanged, so there is no
`contract-ci` ordering between them. SCP-05 (chat, slow mode, tips, DVR, live
ABR) stays deferred. [Sanitized evidence](evidence/a26-rehearsal.json).

Same lab shape as A26: a pipe-only proxy on `127.0.0.1:8099` in front of a
production Next standalone server on `:3100` and a two-process vidra-core
(`VIDRA_ROLE=api` on `:8088`, a separate `VIDRA_ROLE=worker`) over native
postgres 16 at schema 141 and native redis, `STORAGE_BACKEND=local`,
`MALWARE_SCAN_MODE=disabled`, `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false`. The ingest is the
compose `media` service's image, pinned:
`docker image inspect` reads its `RepoDigests` back as
`alfg/nginx-rtmp@sha256:780831ae…6427b513`, the digest in
`docker-compose.yml`. It runs the **shipped**
`deploy/media/nginx.conf.template` with exactly two lines changed — the shim's
api upstream port — plus two deviations stated once here: the control port
`8082` is published to the host (core is on the host, not the compose network,
and the compose service deliberately publishes only 1935), and `--add-host
api:host-gateway` also resolves to an unreachable IPv6 address, so nginx logs
one failed upstream attempt before falling back.

**SC1, module truth — passes, and it is the one thing that was never in doubt.**
`nginx -V` on the pinned image reports `nginx/1.23.1` built
`--add-module=/tmp/nginx-rtmp-module-1.2.2`; `nginx -t` against the shipped
template with only the secret substituted is *syntax is ok / test is
successful*, which by itself proves `rtmp_control` and `rtmp_stat` are compiled
in — nginx refuses an unknown directive. `/stat` answers **200** with
`<nginx_rtmp_version>1.1.4</nginx_rtmp_version>`. A missing or wrong
`X-Ingest-Secret` is **401** on both `/stat` and `/control`, and two
unauthenticated drop attempts against a live publisher left it connected and the
stream `live`. One thing the contract got wrong: a drop that matches nothing
answers **200 with a body of `0`**, not 404, so `ErrIngestNoPublisher` is
unreachable on this build and any 2xx reads as a successful disconnect. That
detail is what made the next defect invisible.

**Defect 1 — the drop never reached the publisher, and the response said it
did.** nginx-rtmp's control and stat modules are **per worker**: each worker
keeps its own stream index, and a control request can only act on publishers
held by whichever worker accepted that HTTP connection. Under the shipped
`worker_processes auto` the streamer's RTMP session lands on one worker and the
api's drop on another. Measured: **twelve consecutive drops** against a live
publisher all answered `0` and the publisher survived every one; consecutive
`/stat` reads on fresh connections came back from **different workers** — pid 11
reported the packaging stream, pid 13 reported an empty server, and the worker
holding the streamer's own socket answered neither. A real moderator termination
returned `publisher_disconnected: true` while the streamer kept going for the
full 60 s the lab watched: **seventeen** new `.ts` segments appeared and the
recording grew **25.8 MB → 38.3 MB**. With `worker_processes 1` the same lab
reads both sessions on every `/stat`, the drop answers `1`, and ffmpeg exits
**0.25 s** later. The ingest transcodes nothing, so one worker is not the
throughput limit an operator meets first.

**Defect 2 — the termination audit row was never written.**
`internal/audit`'s envelope refuses an event that carries a resource id with no
resource type, and `internal/live` discards `Record`'s error on purpose — a
moderation action must never fail because the trail did. `content.live.terminate`
set `ResourceID` and no `ResourceType`, so it was rejected in `normalizeEvent`
and disappeared: no row, no log line. A real termination landed every other
effect — state, key rotation, publisher drop, the creator-visible reason — and
`audit_log` held only `content.live.replay`. **The one thing the hardening said
it fixed about live auditing, putting the stream id in `resource_id` instead of
free text, is exactly what made the row unstorable.** The package's `fakeAuditor`
appended to a slice and never ran the envelope; it now pushes every event
through a real `audit.Service`, and that test change is the durable part.

**Defect 3 — the moderator's dialog could not terminate anything.**
`lib/api/client.ts` JSON-encodes every non-FormData body; `endpoints.ts`'s
`terminateLiveStream` stringified its body first, so what went on the wire was a
JSON **string** whose contents happened to be JSON, and echo's `Bind` refused it
before `Validate` ran — a bare `400 malformed or invalid request body`, not a 422
naming a field. Every click of **End stream** failed. It is the only endpoint in
that file that double-encoded.

**SC2, termination end to end — passes with all three fixed.** A moderator
signed in to Chromium, opened the live watch page, clicked **End stream**, picked
*Breaks the instance rules* and wrote a note. The response is
`200 {"state":"ended","publisher_disconnected":true,"stream_key_rotated":true}`.
**ffmpeg exits 0.08 s after that response** with code 187 and
`Error submitting a packet to the muxer: End of file` → `Error writing trailer` →
`Error closing file` → `Conversion failed!`. The ingest log carries the whole
chain on the one worker: the streamer's socket disconnects, the loopback
packaging push tears down, the `hls` session closes, and
`notify: publish_done '127.0.0.1:8082/ingest/stop'` fires the ordinary stop hook.
Between the click and the exit one in-progress segment grew 6 392 bytes and the
recording 6 807 — the last flush. In the **twelve seconds after the drop nothing
grew and nothing appeared**; the only change under `LIVE_HLS_ROOT` is the `.flv`
disappearing, which is retention 0 deleting it once the replay published. The old
key's next publish is refused at the hook (`404 no live stream for that key`),
the ingest drops the connection, ffmpeg reports `Input/output error`, and the
running publisher is untouched.

The replay is **complete**: 127 s of broadcast produced a **127 s** replay,
`published`, public, on the stream's own channel, with a three-variant CMAF
master answering 200 — `init-0.mp4` plus `chunk-0-00001.m4s` probes as h264
1280×720 30/1, duration 6.000. The audit row now reads
`content.live.terminate / success / user / **live_stream** / <stream-id> /
harassment`.

The creator's stream page and the Studio both say *"This stream was ended by a
moderator: Breaks the instance rules. A26 rehearsal: synthetic termination, no
real content."* from the one copy module; an anonymous visitor reloading the
same page gets only *"This live stream has ended."* — the reason does not leak.
Wrong actors: anonymous **401**, plain user **403**, the stream's own creator
**403** on the admin route, moderator **200**; anonymous **401** and another user
**404** on the owner route, with the state still `live` after every refusal. The
owner's `POST /live/{id}/end` does the same — `publisher_disconnected` and
`stream_key_rotated` true, **0.27 s** to ffmpeg's exit, a 40 s replay for a 39 s
broadcast — and writes **no audit row at all**.

**SC3, viewer count — passes on the API, and the rendered number does not
move.** Three Chromium contexts on distinct client addresses (the pipe proxy is
loopback and therefore trusted, so `ExtractIPFromXFFHeader` returns each
context's own `X-Forwarded-For`): anonymous, signed in with default consent, and
signed in **opted out** of history and personalization. `viewer_count` read
`1, 1, 1, 1, 3` and reached **3** about twelve seconds after the third joined —
the 10 s read cache. Closing one viewer held 3 through 85.2 s and dropped to **2
at 90.2 s**, the documented 90 s window almost exactly. Anonymous and opted-out
viewers are both counted; the field is omitted when the stream is not live.

Two things the count is not. The rendered page shows **`0 viewers` at load and
never updates** — `LiveWatchView` polls only while the state is `offline`, so a
live page fetches the stream once; a reload with three watching shows `3
viewers`. And the signed-in branch of `liveViewerDigest` is **unreachable on a
public stream**: hls.js sends no session credential with the playlist (the only
`Authorization` it carries is a private stream's playback token), so every viewer
digests as `ip:<RealIP>`. Measured directly — an anonymous viewer and a signed-in
viewer on **one** address produced **one** Redis set member and a count of 1.
Viewers behind one NAT count once, and the privacy note's distinction between a
signed-in and an anonymous digest never happens.

**SC4, recording retention — passes in both modes.** At `0`, the `.flv` is gone
from `<LIVE_HLS_ROOT>/rec` as soon as the replay VOD publishes; measured four
times, once as the *only* file change in the twelve seconds after a drop, leaving
`rec/` holding just `.keep`. At `1h` the same broadcast shape published its
replay and left `b49b313c-…-1788892293.flv` (338 836 B) on the volume. The
sweep's selection was exercised against that real file: the worker's loop is
hourly with no cadence knob, so `live.DirRecordingStore.PruneRecordings` was run
directly from a throwaway harness inside the module (deleted afterwards, the
checkout is clean) — a fresh file against a 1 h cutoff selects **0**; the same
file backdated two hours selects and deletes **1**, and `rec/.keep` is untouched.

**SC5, the `live_ingest` component — passes.** With the ingest up, `/readyz` and
`/admin/system` both read `ok` and the component list is now eleven. With the
container **stopped**, both read `live_ingest: down` — *"the RTMP ingest did not
answer its control surface; publishes will be refused and live viewers will see a
dead player"* — the overall status is `degraded`, and **`/readyz` still answers
200** (as does `/healthz`), so one shared ingest cannot empty every replica out.
With `LIVE_RTMP_URL` unset it is `not_configured` and the instance reads `ok`.
With live configured and `LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL` unset it is `not_configured`
*with the explanation* — *"…so the RTMP ingest is never probed and a moderator
cannot disconnect a publisher"*. And a control URL with **no secret** refuses to
boot: exit 1, `config: LIVE_INGEST_SECRET is required when
LIVE_INGEST_CONTROL_URL is set`.

**SC6, re-verified clauses.** A **mid-broadcast key rotation** returns 200 with a
new key, does not disconnect the current publisher (state stays `live`, segments
keep appearing), and the old key's next publish is refused at the hook. The
**duration watchdog** with `live_max_duration_secs = 60` (its floor) force-closed
at **81 s** — the limit plus up to one 30 s sweep — flipped the state, 404d the
playlist and wrote `content.live.force_close / success / system` with
`resource_id` still **empty**; the publisher was **not** disconnected and was
still ingesting after the cut, so the watchdog does not use the control surface
that now exists. **Hooks alone** are still insufficient: a wrong secret and a
missing secret are both 401 with no state change, and a valid hook with no RTMP
publish flips the row `live`, advertises `hls_url` and lists the stream on the
public rail while the playlist answers **404**. **Disconnect → replay** holds: a
SIGKILLed publisher at ~57 s produced `ended`, a 404 live playlist and a 56 s
published replay.

**Gates.** vidra-core `make ci` and PR #211's `ci-required` — pass (no migration;
`api/openapi.yaml` unchanged). vidra-user `npm run ci` on Node 26 and PR #201's
`ci-required`, `frontend`, `contract`, both `e2e-backed` lanes,
`channel-sync-backed` and `ipfs-backed` — pass. vidra-search was not touched.
Meta changes here are documentation only.

**Findings that need a ruling rather than a patch, none blocking the verdict.**
`DropPublisher` cannot tell a real disconnect from "nothing matched" — this
module answers both with 200 and differs only in a body count that is discarded —
so terminating a hook-only phantom session with no publisher at all still reports
`publisher_disconnected: true`; whether a termination should *verify* the drop is
a decision, not a bug fix. The live watch page polls only while `offline`, so a
broadcast's viewer count is a load-time snapshot and a terminated stream does not
flip to its ended state without a reload. The signed-in viewer digest is
unreachable on public streams. An owner's own end writes no audit row of any
kind, and `content.live.terminate` records `actor_kind=user` but leaves
`actor_role` empty. `content.live.replay` and `content.live.force_close` still
carry an empty `resource_id`. A hook-only flip still advertises a byte-less
stream on the public rail; there is still no live ABR ladder and nothing resyncs
a drifted player to the edge.

**Unverified.** No OBS or other real streaming client. The compose `media`
profile was not brought up as a profile — its image, command and shipped template
were reproduced by hand. The hourly retention ticker itself was not waited out
(its selection was run directly). No TLS, no real hostnames, no ingest reachable
from another machine. Replays landed on **local** storage; S3 was not exercised.
The simultaneous-live caps were not exercised, and no run had more than three
concurrent viewers or a viewer on a real remote network.

The lab was torn down: every process, the postgres cluster, the Redis server and
the ingest container were started by this session in a scratch directory and
stopped at the end; the one instance-settings override made during the lab
(`live_max_duration_secs`) was removed, so `instance_settings` is empty again.
Credentials, stream keys, recordings, replays and raw logs stay outside the repo.
## A29 parity — one handle namespace, retroactive blocks, threaded mirror — 2026-09-08

**INT-05 is not re-scored and not flipped.** The A29 rehearsal ("A29 rehearsal —
two instances against the merged remediation") named exactly two sub-clauses of
the row's own procedure as unmet, said they were the same clause, and said they
needed *a ruling, not a patch*. The owner ruled today, and
this is the ruling implemented: accounts and channels share one handle namespace,
and a block is taken against an ACCOUNT and is retroactive. The six smaller
findings that rehearsal recorded without fixing are closed alongside them. Only
the third two-instance run can flip the row, and this section is not it.

**It is code-only, deliberately.** Another executor holds the machine's lab and
Docker, so nothing below has federated between two live instances: every claim
is a test, a migration applied to a real PostgreSQL, or a sentence saying what
was not measured. Complete result:
[`a29-parity.json`](evidence/a29-parity.json). Open on
[vidra-core #210](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/210) and
[vidra-user #202](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/202) — **neither is
merged**, and the user PR stays draft until core lands, because its
`lib/api/generated.ts` is regenerated from core's branch spec and `contract-ci`
fetches the spec from vidra-core's default branch.

### The reservation, and what it does to an existing collision

Migration **0142**. `actor_handles` holds one row per live handle with
`handle_lower` as the PRIMARY KEY and cascading `user_id`/`channel_id` foreign
keys (exactly one set), so a deleted account or channel releases its name with no
application code and no DELETE anywhere in the migration. Two AFTER triggers on
`users(username)` and `channels(handle)` upsert the row, arbitrating on the
SUBJECT index so a rename MOVES the reservation while a cross-kind collision
raises on `actor_handles_pkey`.

They are AFTER triggers for a reason worth stating: a same-kind duplicate must
keep raising on `users_username_lower_idx` / `channels_handle_lower_idx`, which
are checked at INSERT time before any AFTER trigger runs. **Every 409 that
shipped before 0142 is byte-identical after it.** Only the cross-kind collision
is new, and it answers **409 with the stable code `handle_reserved`** — the same
message in both directions, because naming the holding kind would make each form
an oracle for the other namespace and neither caller can act on the distinction
anyway. Normalisation is `lower()`, the normalisation both existing unique
indexes have always used, so the reservation cannot disagree with the uniqueness
that predates it.

Four surfaces, and two of them do not exist yet. Registration and channel
creation refuse; OAuth/ATProto username derivation now probes `actor_handles`
instead of `users`, so a derived name that dodged every account and landed on a
channel handle is skipped by the dedupe loop rather than 409-ing a first sign-in;
and a username change and a channel handle change — neither of which has an
endpoint — are covered by `UPDATE OF` on the same triggers, which is the only
ordering that cannot ship a hole later. A pending registration REQUEST is still
checked at APPROVAL time rather than at submission, exactly as a username already
taken by a user has always been there; that is left as it is and said out loud.

**The backfill renames the channel side, and the account wins every collision** —
a username is a sign-in identifier, so renaming it locks a person out, while
renaming a channel handle changes a URL this migration also keeps alive. The rule
is `<handle>-channel`, then `-channel-2`, `-channel-3`, … until the name is free
of the account namespace, the channel namespace and the aliases already written.
It is a FUNCTION (`backfill_actor_handles()`) rather than an inline `DO` block so
the rule can be exercised on a seeded collision by a test instead of only by the
one run that ever executes it, and it is idempotent. Measured on real PostgreSQL
16.15 at schema 141: user `OwnerA` with channels `ownera` and `ownera-channel` →
`ownera` renamed to **`ownera-channel-2`** because the first candidate was taken,
the account kept `ownera`, one audit row (`content.channel.handle_renamed`,
`reason=from=ownera to=ownera-channel-2`, both names also in `metadata` because
`audit_log` carries no prose), and a second call renamed **0**.

**The alias keeps two different promises with two different lifetimes.** For
humans, `/channels/<old>` answers 301 to the new handle until `expires_at`, one
year from the rename; after that the alias stops resolving and the name is free
for a future channel, which nothing else could have claimed in the meantime
because the account that caused the rename holds the reservation. For peers,
`is_actor_id` marks the one alias the **ActivityPub actor `id` is built from, and
`expires_at` does not apply to it**: the id, inbox, outbox, followers, following
and `publicKey.id` all stay at the OLD handle and only `preferredUsername`
follows the rename. Peers hold `…/video-channels/ownera` in their follow rows, in
their cached actors and in every activity's `attributedTo`; an id that changes
underneath them is an actor that silently ceases to exist. An alias is a courtesy
to humans and expires; a federated id is a promise to other servers and does not.
The frozen identity lives in the alias table rather than as a `channels` column
because adding one turned every channel query whose SELECT lists the table's
columns into a bespoke sqlc row type — measured, then reverted.

### WebFinger answers both actors

`acct:name@domain` returns the Person as `rel=self` and the Group as
`rel=alternate`, both `type: application/activity+json`, so a peer picks by type
instead of taking whichever this server happened to try first. A name held by
only one kind still answers with exactly one link at `rel=self` — the shipped
shape, unchanged, so a peer that understands only `self` is unaffected. `self` is
the Person because RFC 7033 makes `self` singular and a bare `acct:` most often
means an account. A renamed channel's OLD name resolves too, through its alias,
at the frozen id: that is the address every existing follower holds.

### The block model, and what it hides

A block names the **ACCOUNT**. A handle resolves through WebFinger and then UP
through the Group's `attributedTo`; a supplied URL climbs the same edge through
the actor CACHE only. `remote_actor_block_reach` — one view, so the ten
viewer-facing queries that ask "is this actor blocked for this reader" cannot
drift apart — expands each block down to every channel actor the account owns and
unions the admin's instance-wide blocks in as rows with a NULL `blocker_id`, so
one predicate answers both scopes and an anonymous reader keeps the admin half.
Naming the account is what makes a channel the person creates TOMORROW blocked
too, which a per-channel row could never do.

Two guards are load-bearing rather than incidental. `attributedTo` is text a
remote server controls, so **only a same-host owner is stored and it is
re-checked at resolution** — a Group claiming an owner elsewhere would otherwise
let a stranger redirect a block, or attach its actors to a well-behaved
instance's account. And **a supplied URL is still never dereferenced**: a handle
has already cost a WebFinger fetch, so one actor fetch on that path changes
nothing about what a caller can make this server do, while a URL has cost nothing
and dereferencing it would turn "block this actor" into "make my server fetch
this address". An unresolvable or unowned actor keeps the URL it was given —
which is exactly the block that was already possible, so the worst case is no
worse than before.

`GET/POST/DELETE /api/v1/admin/federation/blocked-actors` is the same control at
the instance's scope, behind `requireRole(admin, moderator)`, so removing one
hostile person no longer means defederating the server they live on and every
creator on it. Audit rows are `moderation.remote_actor.block` / `.unblock` with
`resource_type=remote_actor` and the actor URL as `resource_id`; the moderator's
note stays on the row and out of the trail.

Per scope, and every row of it reversible because hiding is a READ filter and
nothing is deleted to hide it:

| what | viewer block | admin per-actor block | admin instance block |
|---|---|---|---|
| the account's EXISTING comments on local videos | hidden for that viewer | hidden for **everyone**, anonymous included | already hidden (unchanged) |
| its channels' comments | hidden for that viewer | hidden for everyone | already hidden |
| the mirrored thread on remote videos | hidden for that viewer | hidden for everyone | already hidden |
| its channels' remote videos in feeds | hidden for that viewer | hidden for everyone | already hidden |
| inbound `Create{Note}` / `Follow` from the account or its channels | refused | refused | refused |
| other viewers, anonymous readers | unaffected | affected (that is the scope) | affected |
| unblock | restores every row exactly | restores every row exactly | restores every row exactly |

Notifications and mentions are governed by the A12 local block→remove ruling and
are unchanged: notifications key on `users.id` and a remote commenter has
`author_id NULL`, so there is no remote notification row to filter. **Hiding a
blocked remote account's videos from vidra-search results is a recorded
follow-up, not a claim** — remote videos are not in the search index's document
model and the k-anon/opt-out seam from A13 lives on the search side. Core's own
`SearchPublicVideos` feed query does carry the reach predicate.

`RemoteVideo` gains `actor_url`, `account_actor_url` and `channel_handle`,
because the remote watch view carried `domain`, `object_url` and `watch_url` and
**no actor identity at all** — so the page offers "Block account" beside Report
and Mute instance, sends the owning account when the origin named one and the
channel actor otherwise, and unblocks with the same URL verbatim.

### The six smaller findings

| # | finding | what it is now |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | the mirrored thread was FLAT — only Notes replying to the video object were stored, so every deeper reply was delivered successfully and dropped silently | `remote_video_comments.parent_object_url` carries the ORIGIN's parent id (replies arrive in any order, so a self-referencing FK would refuse one whose parent has not arrived); the origin-authority check still runs against the VIDEO's origin, so a third instance cannot answer into a thread it does not host |
| (b) | a Follow refused during an instance block left the SENDER's row `pending` forever, and a Reject DELETED the row, making a refusal indistinguishable from a follow never made | `remote_channel_follows.state` is **pending \| accepted \| rejected**; `rejected` is terminal and creator-visible, and re-following re-arms it to `pending` with a NEW Follow activity id — one deliberate retry, and the only path back for the blocked case |
| (c) | `FederationHealth.LastDeliveredAt` was computed on every probe and rendered into nothing | `ComponentStatus` gains an optional `detail` map; the federation component sets `pending`, `dead_lettered` and — only when something has been delivered — `last_delivered_at`, and the admin card renders it on healthy AND failing rows, saying "never" when absent rather than printing a zero timestamp |
| (d) | worker-queued federation deliveries carried no request id on either row | `jobtrace.Recorder.RunContext` reads the originating ids back off the run the worker is executing, wired into the transcode completion hook (which is what queues them) and into `uploadfinalize`; a live request wins, an unknown run invents nothing |
| (e) | the 410 Tombstone carried an ETag | gone — and it is worse than meaningless: an ETag invites `If-None-Match`, and a 304 on a 410 would tell the peer that what it already holds, the video, is current |
| (f) | `DELETE /admin/instances/blocked/{domain}` refused a percent-encoded colon | `domainParam()` percent-decodes the segment on the mute, unmute and unblock routes, so both spellings are the same request; an undecodable segment passes through unchanged and the validator refuses it with the message it already has |

### Gates

`vidra-core`: `make ci` **PASS** (fmt-check, vet, migrate-lint — 142 up
migrations clean, openapi-verify, sqlc-verify, test-race). `ci-required` **green**,
including `prev-release-against-new-schema` — see "The compat collision, and the
ruling on it" below for the one accepted break it now carries and how it clears
itself. `go vet
-tags=integration ./...` clean. `go test -tags=integration -count=1 -p 1
./internal/federation/... ./internal/store/...` **ok** against a FRESH
PostgreSQL 16.15 (Homebrew, native — no Docker was used) migrated 0→142 and a
native Redis; `./internal/httpapi/... ./cmd/api/... ./internal/video/...` ok
too. Migration 0142 was applied and REVERSED against that database, on an empty
schema and on one seeded with a collision.

Two pre-existing integration fixtures gave a channel its owner's **exact**
username — the collision the namespace now refuses, and precisely the shape the
backfill renames on a real instance. They derive a handle instead; that is a
fixture correction, and it is the first thing this rule found in our own tree.

`vidra-user`: `npm run ci` **PASS** on Node 26.8.1 / npm 11.19.0 — typecheck,
lint (0 errors, 2 pre-existing warnings), lint:icons, **2587 vitest tests in 258
files**, `next build`, **627 Playwright e2e**. `lib/api/generated.ts` regenerated
from core's branch spec and committed.

This repo: evidence only; `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p '*_test.py'`
**OK (48 tests)**.

### Unverified, and named rather than skipped

**Nothing here has federated.** No two-instance run, no browser, no Caddy — this
slice is code-only by instruction. The 301 alias redirect exists in the data
model and its resolution is tested, but no HTTP client has followed one.
Interoperability is unverified: no PeerTube or Mastodon has seen a two-link
WebFinger answer (both accept a single `rel=self` link, which is what a name held
by one kind still returns). The backfill has run against seeded fixtures only,
never against beta's real data. MIG-06's identity clause, signed fetch on the
object routes and F8 authoring all stay deferred, unchanged.

### What the third two-instance run must prove

A viewer on B blocks `@name@A` from the remote watch page's own control, and A's
channel videos AND its already-stored comments leave that viewer's surfaces while
another viewer on B still sees both. The same block taken by B's admin hides them
for an anonymous reader too, and the unblock restores every row. A's WebFinger
answers a colliding name with both links and B follows the GROUP from it — the
request the rehearsal watched sit `pending` forever. A reply to a mirrored comment
lands on B and renders under its parent. A Reject leaves B's row `rejected` rather
than gone, and re-following sends a fresh Follow. A private and an unlisted upload
still produce ZERO activities (core #209's clause, merged and untouched here).
`/admin/system`'s federation card shows a real `last_delivered_at` and
`/admin/jobs` shows a request id on a delivery queued by a transcode completion.
The 410 Tombstone carries no ETag through the edge, and
`DELETE /admin/instances/blocked/<host%3Aport>` answers 204.

## Live follow-ups — verified drop, watchdog disconnect, audited ends, polling watch view — 2026-09-08

**INT-01 does not move.** It is already PASS, and nothing here re-measures it —
that takes the publisher, the ingest container and the browser back. What this
slice does is take four of the five findings the A26 rehearsal recorded as
"needing a ruling rather than a patch" and build the rulings. Two code PRs
([core #212](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-core/pull/212),
[user #203](https://github.com/yegamble/vidra-user/pull/203)) and this one; no
migration (core stays at schema 141), one `api/openapi.yaml` **description**
change, so user #203 carries the contract regen and stays a draft until core
merges. Everything below is **not lab-observed**.
[Sanitized evidence](evidence/live-follow-ups.json).

**A drop that dropped nothing said it had.** nginx-rtmp answers
`/control/drop/publisher` with **200 and a decimal count**, including `0` when
the name matches nothing — not the `404` the shipped contract was written
against. `DropPublisher` read the status and discarded the body, so every 2xx
became a confirmed disconnect. That is what made A26's headline defect
invisible: twelve consecutive drops that were reaching a different nginx worker
than the one holding the socket all answered `0`, all read as success, and the
